title: Remembering Has a Price: Learning Memory Worth under Resource Constraints
abstract: Lifelong agents continually accumulate and reuse experience to improve after deployment, yet in practice they often operate under tight generation, interaction, and memory budgets. Under such stringent joint constraints, we find that existing lifelong-memory methods can become ineffective, with several sophisticated approaches offering little advantage over simple retrieval or even no-memory agents. This reveals a more fundamental problem: resource scarcity makes each memory decision more consequential. When only a small amount of past experience can be retained or reused and opportunities for reasoning and recovery are limited, retrieving a relevant but ineffective memory can consume scarce context and hinder downstream execution. The key challenge is therefore not simply to retrieve relevant experience, but to determine which experiences are actually worth retaining and reusing. To address this challenge, we propose TokenWorth, a lightweight online memory framework that learns query-dependent memory worth from sparse execution feedback and applies it consistently to memory retrieval and bounded memory management. Across three LifelongAgentBench environments and both local and API-based deployments, TokenWorth achieves the highest task success rate while using the fewest output tokens among the evaluated methods. These results suggest that effective lifelong adaptation under resource constraints depends not on remembering more, but on learning what is worth remembering. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/AIGNLAI/TokenWorth.

title: Research Log: reproducible experiments on LLM agents, air quality and AI in public services
abstract: Small, reproducible experiments run on a laptop: a ReAct agent with a 3B local model on English and Roman Urdu questions, including a name-swap robustness check; one year of PM2.5 data for Lahore and six Pakistani cities against the WHO guideline; and a base-rate model of AI road-safety camera flags in the UK. Code is MIT-licensed; third-party data keeps its original licence.

title: Tandem: Serving Hybrid Linear-Attention GUI Agents on Mobile NPUs
abstract: Smartphone GUI agents complete tasks in mobile apps by repeatedly reading the screen and asking a model for the next action. Mobile neural processing units (NPUs) enable local execution, keeping screen contents on the phone, but model latency accumulates with every action. Hybrid linear attention models reduce memory requirements, yet reusing their recurrent state requires checkpoints at the appropriate input positions. Agent requests retain instructions but rewrite recent history, so checkpoint policies designed for chat continuation can miss reusable prefixes. Retaining rollback states for speculative decoding can also move prompt processing off the NPU's matrix unit, adding overhead that outweighs decoding savings on short action outputs. A loaded model can further hold the NPU awake between tasks. We present Tandem, a runtime for hybrid GUI agents on mobile NPUs. Tandem saves recurrent state where consecutive prompts diverge, allowing later requests to reuse previously processed context. It keeps most prefill on the matrix unit and produces rollback states through a short per-token tail. Its verification kernel reads each weight block once for all proposed tokens. Between request bursts, Tandem releases NPU power votes without unloading the model. We implement Tandem in llama.cpp and evaluate it on recorded agent interactions across two Snapdragon generations. On a Snapdragon 8 Elite, Tandem reduces per-step latency by 30% for text-based screen descriptions and 16% for screenshots relative to llama.cpp's fastest NPU configuration, reduces energy per text step by 33%, and lowers standby power with the model loaded from 0.76 to 0.22 W.

title: HarnessRL: Co-Evolving Policies with a Just-in-Time Training Harness for Open-Ended RL
abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) trains policies for open-ended generation with natural-language criteria as rewards, but these rewards can become ineffective as training progresses. We identify two failure modes. Under non-discriminative rewards, scores collapse to uniformly low or high values due to insufficient exploration or a mismatch between task difficulty and policy capability. Under spurious rewards, higher scores do not correspond to better responses. Both reflect a training configuration whose task sampling, exploration, and evaluation stay fixed as the policy evolves. We introduce HarnessRL, a training-time harness that co-evolves with the policy through three interfaces for task sampling, rollout guidance, and rubric criteria. HarnessRL maintains a training-time memory from which a harness evolver retrieves within-task history and cross-task evidence. Using this evidence, the evolver attributes each reward failure to the interface whose update can address it. It then runs a proposer and just-in-time critic loop in which the critic accepts a candidate update only after measuring its effect on the current frozen policy, returning rejected candidates for revision. We also curate Rubric-Mix-10k, a five-domain training and evaluation suite for open-ended RL across medical, science, writing, role-play, and instruction-following tasks. On Rubric-Mix-10k, HarnessRL outperforms the strongest baselines by 2.8 to 3.1 points across both 4B and 9B model scales and nearly halves the training steps to its best checkpoint. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Tongyi-ConvAI/Qwen-Character/tree/main/HarnessRL.

title: A CTCM-ALA Adaptive Embedded Fusion Optimization Method for UAV Path Planning in Complex Medical Rescue Environments
abstract: To improve the accuracy and safety margin deficiencies of unmanned aerial vehicles in autonomous medical emergency search-and-rescue missions, this paper develops an adaptive embedded fusion optimizer named CTCM-ALA for rescue UAV path planning. The proposed algorithm hybridizes the tribe-competition member-cooperation strategy and artificial lemming algorithm to construct hierarchically adaptive initial populations, speed up convergence and prevent local convergence traps. Tests on 12 CEC2017 functions prove its better optimization performance. Real-world applications in dense urban and complicated topographic medical rescue cases verify its reliability and precision.

title: How Benchmark Graph Construction Shapes Multi-Hop KG Navigation: A Controlled Audit of PathQuestion and PathQuestion-Large
abstract: Multi-hop knowledge-graph question answering (KGQA) benchmarks are often treated as fixed language-and-reasoning tasks, but for navigation-based methods, difficulty also depends on the graph in which those tasks are instantiated. This makes graph construction a consequential but often entangled part of the navigation task. To isolate this effect, we audit PathQuestion (PQ) and PathQuestion-Large (PQL) as graph-navigation benchmarks under a controlled intervention: we hold questions, topic entities, released answers, released path annotations, and family-level splits fixed while replacing each released task-filtered graph with the larger source KG distributed with the benchmark. Source restoration expands the effective navigation search space and graph-consistent answer and path multiplicity while sharply reducing unguided reachability to released answers. We evaluate whether these structural changes persist across navigation policies using structural references, frozen small-language-model navigation policies, and trained MINERVA policies. Across both frozen and trained policies, restoration substantially reduces released-answer accuracy and trajectory fidelity, while graph-consistent evaluation recovers only part of the loss. These results show that benchmark graph construction is part of the navigation task specification rather than merely an implementation detail and can materially shape measured behavior even when the released QA task is held fixed.

title: The Development of Sycophancy in Language Models: Tracing Vulnerabilities from Pretraining to Post-Training
abstract: Language models can change a committed answer to accommodate a user's opinion or pushback without new evidence. However, when this behaviour develops during training and what a released model inherits from earlier stages remain unclear. We follow 741 checkpoints of 30 open model lineages, from early pretraining to released models. We plant initial verdicts on moral scenarios and measure how far a model follows a user's stated opinion or abandons its verdict under pressure. In most lineages the behaviour is present before post-training, and its average strength changes in either direction, at different stages across lineages. A clearer pattern emerges at the level of individual questions. Beyond responses without pressure, pretraining behaviour predicts little of which questions a released model yields on. That pattern forms during post-training: on routes with supervised fine-tuning, the fine-tuning checkpoint predicts part of it and the preference-optimization checkpoint most of it. A sibling trained from the same base along another route predicts far less: for Tülu-3 8B, its own preference-stage checkpoint removes 85% of the remaining prediction error, a sibling 19%. Internal states add predictive information without changing this ranking. Similar average scores conceal different vulnerabilities, and training history matters for auditing a released model.

title: GAIDA: Generative AI for Human-in-the-Loop Document Annotation
abstract: Document annotation is a fundamental yet labor-intensive step in building document information extraction systems. While Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Large Language Models (LLMs) can automate parts of this process, we argue that annotation systems should be judged not by how completely they remove human effort, but by how effectively they redirect it toward review and correction. We propose a modular human-in-the-loop architecture that integrates OCR-based extraction, LLM-based semantic pre-annotation, and human validation in a single editable workflow, and present GAIDA, a research prototype serving as its reference implementation. GAIDA supports interchangeable OCR engines, LLM backends, and prompt configurations, and enables stage-specific measurement of annotation effort. In an initial single-annotator, stage-specific study on the FUNSD scanned-form and WildReceipt retail-receipt benchmarks, OCR assistance reduced region-creation and transcription time by up to 80.9\%, and reviewing LLM pre-annotations reduced semantic-labeling time by up to 73.7\%, despite imperfect pre-annotations of 78.86\% and 86.98\% Micro F1 on FUNSD and WildReceipt, respectively. Finally, we reuse the same implementation, adapting only OCR and prompt configuration, to build and openly release AraReceipt, a manually annotated dataset of 100 Arabic receipt images labeled with 25 key-information classes. The results indicate that imperfect automated outputs provide practical value when presented as editable suggestions under human control.

title: Privacy-Preserving Speaker Verification via Content Separation Using Residual Vector Quantization
abstract: 본 논문에서는 프라이버시 보존 화자검증 프레임 워크를 제안한다. 제안하는 프레임워크는 잔차 벡터 양자화 기반 신경망 오디오 코덱을 활용하여 화자 정보와 음성 콘텐츠를 분리한다. 구체적으로, 음성 신호를 내용 토큰과 음향 토큰으로 분리하고, 음향 토큰에 전역 셔플링을 적용하여 언어적 내용 정보를 제거한다. 이 후 셔플링된 음향 토큰을 입력으로 화자 검증 모델을 학습한다. 제안 방법은 기존 코덱 기반 방법 대비 높은 내용 복원 불가능성(WER 99.98%)을 달성하면서도 경쟁력 있는 화자검증 성능 (EER 5.19%) 을 유지함을 확인하였다.

title: The Effectiveness and Durability of Pretraining Data Filtering in Protein Language Models
abstract: Pretraining filtering is one of the most common safeguards for open-weight language models. Here we study its effectiveness, durability and scalability using the ESM-2 family of protein language models. We find that filtering viral proteins from the pretraining data meaningfully degrades masked language modelling, mutation effect prediction and long-range contact prediction on viral proteins, while largely preserving performance on non-viral proteins. These effects are concentrated among proteins from human-infecting viruses, and grow as we scale models from 8M to 3B parameters. As models increase in size, we find that stringent filtering becomes more effective. However, fine-tuning on sequences from the removed viral families restores the lost performance. Although the cost to recover performance increases with model scale, even for the largest models it costs about 80 USD of H100 time. This work establishes pretraining filtering as moderately effective at selectively degrading performance on viral proteins, but not durable against fine-tuning with modest computational resources and access to relevant data.

title: Simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation for stochastic reaction networks
abstract: Uncovering stochastic reaction networks from data is central to single-cell biology. Simulation-based inference has evolved into a flexible paradigm for this purpose, circumventing the computational intractability of the likelihood. Notably, approximate Bayesian computation performs this inference by carrying out extensive Gillespie simulations, usually at a high computational cost. Here, we propose a simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation (SFABC) framework that avoids both simulation and explicit likelihood solutions of the network dynamics. Instead, SFABC exploits the Chemical Master Equation to formulate a tractable convex optimization with ensuing constraints, which are then used to accept sampled parameters consistent with the observed data. The resulting posterior approximation comes with theoretical guarantees: it can be tightened systematically, and it provably converges to the exact Bayesian posterior distributions. Using synthetic benchmarks, we show that SFABC matches the accuracy of standard simulation-based algorithms at a substantially reduced computational cost. We then showcase the applicability of SFABC to experimental systems biology by analyzing gene transcription bursting kinetics from snapshot, time-resolved, and cell-cycle-resolved single-cell data.

title: From Outcomes to Components: A Counterfactual Evaluation Framework for LLM-Proposed Repairs
abstract: An LLM-generated repair action specifies which records to change and by how much. A failed action may still contain a useful target set or numerical update, depending on how the two are paired. We evaluate this problem in traffic networks and databases, where aggregate observations obscure the records that need correction. We examine the pairings by executing each combination from the same initial state, using a reference action that restores the affected records. title: The Control Layer Behind Rule-Following Agents Trading Across Market Conditions
abstract: Trading discipline often fails people. Our study tested whether four AI trading agents followed their strategies and risk rules. Offering traders the evidence and an agent evaluation toolkit to separate luck from following the rules, before giving agents meaningful autonomy or capital. Our study analysed 2,627 closed positions from 12 February to 27 August 2026 across the same asset universe and execution conditions. Most positions were simulated against live prices with a 0.09% round-trip fee; 18% involved real Hyperliquid orders. Each position declared a strategy, stop and target, with a limit of five open positions per agent. The fleet finished net positive after fees. Rule adherence was high across all four agents, including the unprofitable one. Profitability tracked how often agents won relative to their break-even win rates. Institutional-style controls ran by default and contained losses through a 29% market drawdown and recovery, with documented exceptions. The discipline held for all four agents. Agents kept 97.5% of gross loss within declared stops, and typical losses closed at declared levels. Declared risk remained stable after losses and broadly stable across calm and volatile months. Twenty-three of 24 runs respected the position limit; logs identify the exception's size and duration. The same live data produced different results across assigned strategies. The trade-log tests can be rerun from the published trade snapshot; regime tests also require the published Bitcoin prices and regime labels. Section 3.5 specifies the stop-breach tolerance. These trade-level results are not account-level returns or proof of a lasting edge. Our study provides an evaluation toolkit to help traders distinguish rule-following from luck before committing capital. For anyone considering allocating capital to agents to trade, discipline should be the entry test, not the only test.

title: LLM-Based Satellite Multimodal Knowledge Graph Construction: A Context-Aware Self-Interpretable Paradigm
abstract: This paper addresses three main bottlenecks in commercial aerospace multimodal data: semantic alignment difficulties, rigid ontologies, and context loss. We propose a method to construct satellite multimodal knowledge graphs (KGs) using Large Language Model (LLM).The process begins with layout analysis. This step preprocesses interleaved text-image satellite documents to align cross-modal semantics. To resolve ambiguity in technical terms, we developed a triple-positioning entity extraction mechanism. This mechanism directly identifies the original text, summaries, and entity types. For event nodes, we use an event-centric modeling paradigm. This paradigm captures spatio-temporal elements and other meta informations to ensure the nodes are self-interpretable. Entity normalization and automatic schema recognition rely on deep vector embedding. This embedding can semantic clustering the entities for the KG, eliminates the need for prior ontologies. We tested the method on real satellite datasets. The experimental results show high logical integrity and confirm its practical value for aerospace failure analysis.

title: Reasoning-Aware Multicalibrated Reliability Predictors for Language Models
abstract: As people increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) for information, model providers need to communicate meaningful estimates of whether individual responses are correct or, more generally, reliable. In the context of hallucinations, existing work uses multicalibration to make such reliability predictions meaningful across application-relevant groups, such as prompt topics. Topic groups alone, however, can conceal systematic errors: within the same topic and confidence level, responses with different chain-of-thought (CoT) properties may exhibit opposing errors that cancel on average. In this work, we introduce reasoning-aware multicalibration, a framework that supplements application-relevant topic groups with groups derived from observable properties of CoT traces. We highlight that, theoretically, groupings based on CoT are "internally important", i.e., groupings for which the multicalibration guarantee is not societally crucial as it is for high-risk topics, but whose inclusion in the multicalibration procedure could easily and significantly improve predictive accuracy of the final reliability predictor. Empirically, we apply our framework to hallucination prediction and unsafe-response detection across a variety of benchmarks, and find that adding CoT groups to topic-based calibration reduces Brier score in both tasks. Interestingly, we find that multicalibrating with respect to CoT groups alone (without any topic information) already improves calibration across topics, suggesting that the predictor's errors depend on how the model reasoned, rather than what it was asked about in the prompt.

title: Selective Transfer through Sequence Distillation: From Benchmark Knowledge to Backdoor Behaviour
abstract: Knowledge distillation is widely used to transfer capabilities from teacher models to student models, but recent work shows that it can also transfer unintended teacher properties. We study whether different hidden teacher properties survive the same distillation channels. Specifically, we compare two properties: benchmark-associated knowledge and refusal backdoors, and show that distillation treats them very differently. Teachers fine-tuned on benchmark data successfully pass that knowledge to students through all four distillation channels we test, including when students are trained only on teacher-generated number sequences containing no natural language or domain content whatsoever. Refusal backdoors tell the opposite story: backdoored teachers achieve near-perfect triggered refusal, yet sequence-distilled students inherit essentially none of this behaviour. Logit-based distillation transfers it substantially, reaching up to 85.5\% triggered refusal in students that saw zero backdoor examples. Distillation is therefore selective, and the selection criterion is not what data the student sees, but what structure the teacher's property has. The code is available at https://github.com/MJonibek/kd-leakage.

title: Reproduction Package for Statistically Certified Explanations
abstract: This archive holds the replication package of a manuscript under review. The package contains the implementation, the scripts behind the manuscript's experiments and figures, a test suite that checks the reported numbers against the code, and a README with installation and run instructions. This archive contains no datasets. The experiments use public corpora that are downloaded separately from their public sources. The README gives the download commands, and a checksum file in the archive verifies the downloads.

title: Dual-Scale Condition-Shift Editing for Robust Real-World Image Demoiréing
abstract: Robust demoiréing of screen-recaptured images remains challenging: moiré varies in frequency, color, and spatial support across display-camera pairs and capture conditions. Dedicated restoration networks trained on finite paired data struggle with this diversity, especially when low-frequency color banding and high-frequency stripes co-occur. We present DemoiréEdit, a content-preserving editing framework that adapts the natural-image prior of a pretrained flow-matching editor to demoiréing. First, an endpoint-supervised training objective supplements velocity matching with pixel, perceptual, and frequency-domain restoration losses. Second, a dual-scale condition-shift strategy performs global correction at low resolution, then refines the image at full resolution by shifting the denoising condition from the first-stage output to the original input for detail recovery. We also introduce DailyMoiré130, a benchmark of challenging moiré in everyday screen photography, comprising 130 smartphone captures across diverse displays with low-frequency color banding, fine high-frequency stripes, and mixed-frequency interference. On the challenging DailyMoiré130 benchmark, our method achieves the lowest residual moiré area and receives 71.3% overall-quality preference in a blind Best-of-7 study with 31 participants. We also evaluate on paired FHDMi/UHDM, reducing residual moiré confidence by 47.1%/9.3% and increasing MUSIQ by 4.3%/2.0% over the best baseline for each metric.

title: A Pitfall in the Evaluation of Gene Perturbation Models
abstract: Gene perturbation models aim to predict transcriptional responses to unseen genetic interventions, but comparisons rely on heterogeneous evaluation metrics and differentially-expressed (DE) gene subsets. We investigate the consequences of these choices using eight methods across six single-gene perturbation datasets under a unified evaluation protocol. Varying the number of top DE genes reveals substantial instability in Precision-based rankings, with the winning method changing 86.7% of the time, while rankings based on the rest of the metrics remain comparatively stable. Investigating this discrepancy exposes that repeating a single predicted expression profile across cell-level rows, a standard practice for many methods, can inflate significance estimates and produce excessively large predicted significant-DE sets. Specifically we found that 67.1% of tested perturbation--gene pairs pass the significance threshold despite some of them having minuscule effects. We derive an inflation factor showing that replicated predictions can amplify the standardized Mann--Whitney statistic even after correction for tied ranks, without adding independent information. This artifact changes Precision mainly as the number of DE genes increases because for smaller cutoffs, most of the genes are already significant due to the effect-based ordering. Taking this pitfall into account in our benchmark comparison, we find that a random forest using Gene Ontology features achieves the best overall results.

title: COVFIRM: Replication Package for "From Recognition to Triggering: Measuring Two Gaps in Agentic Firmware Analysis"
abstract: This replication package accompanies “From Recognition to Triggering: Measuring Two Gaps in Agentic Firmware Analysis.” The Inspect archive provides the English manuscript, figures, derived result tables, static-bridge artifacts, and a SHA-256 file manifest. The Recompute archive adds selected path-sanitized saved inputs and scripts for four documented offline commands. All four commands passed on an extracted copy, and all 21 regenerated derived CSV tables matched the archived versions byte for byte. The package supports inspection and bounded offline recomputation of the reported results. Complete raw dynamic replay logs and emulator images are not included. Consult the READMEs and manifests for commands and provenance. CC BY 4.0 applies to original materials the COVFIRM authors have authority to license; embedded third-party material retains its original rights.

title: Revision-Based Learning from Interactive Experience and Feedback
abstract: Code generation models are increasingly used to produce interactive artifacts, such as websites and user interfaces. Many properties that determine whether these interfaces are useful only become apparent through realistic interaction, making them difficult to incorporate into model training. In this paper, we introduce RELIEF (REvision-based Learning from Interactive Experience and Feedback), a method for improving code generation models using feedback on their generated interfaces. RELIEF uses a coding agent to revise these interfaces, then incorporates the improvements into their original generation traces to produce supervision for fine-tuning. To evaluate RELIEF, we collected a dataset of 200 synthetically generated websites paired with 355 interaction recordings and accompanying feedback from 24 users. We used critiques derived from code inspection, automated interaction, explicit human feedback, and human interaction recordings to fine-tune variants of two code generation models. Our results show that feedback effectiveness varies with base model capabilities, with critiques inferred from human interaction recordings leading to the largest usability improvements overall under our tested models.

title: XGLASS: X-Ray, Gaze and Language Assisted Slice Sequencing for CT Volumes
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) achieve remarkable performance on 2D medical images, such as X-rays or pathology images, while 3D VLMs that directly process CT/MRI volumes lag behind due to limited 3D training data and the predominance of 2D foundation architectures. To leverage powerful 2D VLMs for analyzing medical volumes, which contain hundreds of slices, it is therefore necessary to focus only on those few slices, which are diagnostically relevant. To enable such a prioritization, we propose XGLASS, a method that transfers medical expertise from 2D X-rays to 3D CT for task-aware slice prioritization. XGLASS uses disease-conditioned importance maps derived from language-aligned radiologist gaze on X-rays and spatially aligns them with coronal CT projections, bringing gaze priors and CT content into a shared 2D representation. The fused gaze-prior/CT projection is then used to predict a disease-specific ordering of axial slices, prioritizing diagnostically relevant slices. XGLASS significantly improves budgeted retrieval over 2D and 3D-native baselines, achieving a top-10 hit rate up to 75.9% for the best-performing disease. In practice, this means that after inspecting only the top 10 slices (4.17% of a 240-slice scan), XGLASS identifies a diagnostically relevant slice in more than 75% of cases. For downstream slice-wise finding classification, an XGLASS-selected 30-slice candidate set reduces model calls by 87.5% while improving F1 by 11.3 percentage points over all-slice inference, 4.2 points over the strongest 2D selector, and remains competitive with 3D-native selectors while requiring up to 130.8 times less time and 10.9 times less GPU memory per finding, supporting its use as a lightweight preselector for volumetric CT analysis. The code and pretrained checkpoint are available on https://github.com/michaelgloeckler/XGLASS.

title: When the harness decides success: state that cannot be re-observed
abstract: Agent harnesses decide what a language model sees across turns: they drop old turns, summarize them, or replay the model's own earlier reasoning. We ask when these choices change whether an agent succeeds, not only what it costs, and report three findings. First, in a pre-registered synthetic probe, truncating the context window costs a low-cost reasoning model nothing in success when a needed fact can be looked up again (it looks the fact up instead), but drops its success to chance when the fact cannot be re-observed: the two penalties differ by 92.5 percentage points (90% CI [89.5, 95.5]). A pre-registered replication on one model from a second provider showed the same contrast. Once the fact was lost, that model chose no answer rather than guessing. Second, on ARC-AGI-3, where the benchmark's Standard harness trails its Provider Adapter harness by a wide margin, we decompose that gap one component at a time, for one model on four games. Summarizing old turns instead of dropping them, while keeping the Standard harness's invitation to take notes, recovers 86% of a 63-point gap without replaying the model's reasoning. The same harness without the invitation recovers 43%, and adding the provider's native replay of the model's reasoning recovers the remaining 57%. These are point estimates from one counted run per configuration and game, and the replay share depends on a single run. Third, in the benchmark's published runs and in ours, the Adapter's advantage in the probability of clearing a level it has reached is larger at deep levels than at early ones. This largely restates where runs stopped and does not separate a growing advantage from a constant one.

title: RoAR-VAE: Improving Latent Diffusability through Robust Prediction
abstract: An effective visual tokenizer must preserve image fidelity while producing latents that downstream diffusion models can learn efficiently. Prior work improves latent diffusability through semantic alignment or joint tokenizer--diffusion training. Revisiting REPA-E, a representative approach, we find that removing its diffusion objective and dedicated generative blocks while retaining semantic prediction from corrupted latents yields comparable downstream generation performance under a matched setting. This observation motivates a general principle of robust prediction: generation-relevant information should remain recoverable from corrupted latents. We instantiate this principle with two complementary objectives. RobustAlign predicts pretrained semantic features from corrupted latents to preserve high-level structure, while RobustRecon reconstructs the clean image to retain fine-grained spatial and appearance information. Together, they form Robust Alignment and Reconstruction VAE (RoAR-VAE). Our analysis suggests that robust prediction improves diffusability by making useful information more accessible in high-variance latent directions, which diffusion models tend to learn earlier. Empirically, RoAR-VAE improves average generation benchmark performance by 2.19 points over the strongest baseline tokenizer under the same training budget, while improving small-text reconstruction accuracy by 16.93 percentage points over FLUX.1-VAE. These results demonstrate that RoAR-VAE achieves a favorable balance between reconstruction fidelity and downstream generative learnability.

title: LeanFlow MCP: A Systems and Formal Verification Architecture for Computer-Assisted Proofs, Exact-Rational Spectral Bounds, and Residue-Arithmetic Certificates in Lean 4
abstract: Interactive Theorem Proving (ITP) & Formal Verification Systems Architecture (5-Round Peer-Reviewed Edition): Presents the architecture, canonical specification lock, and verification suite of LeanFlow MCP (leanflow_mcp), an automated reasoning and formal verification framework in Lean 4 (v4.34.1, zero sorryAx, zero custom axioms) that certifies numerical solver outputs via exact rational arithmetic (Q) and multi-modular Residue Number System (RNS) Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) witnesses. Demonstrates 5 machine-checked modules: (1) Theorem 2.1 (leanflow_cap_galerkin_radii_polynomial_contraction): operator-derived Newton-Kantorovich radii-polynomial bounds (Y_0, Z_0, Z_1, Z_tail, Z_2) = (1/10000, 7/20, 1/200, 1/200, 12) from a 3D Fourier-Galerkin vorticity system (nu = 1/100, M = 10, lambda_M = 1, C_Sob = 1/200), certifying finite-mode (kappa_fin = 181/500 = 0.362), continuum (kappa_tot = 93/250 = 0.372, P_cont(10^-3) = -33/62500 < 0), and self-similar (kappa_ss = 443/1000 = 0.443) contractions; (2) Lemma 2.2 (leanflow_piecewise_scale_involution_lemma) & Lemma 2.3 (leanflow_smooth_vs_piecewise_characterization_lemma): piecewise vs. smooth scale-dual algebraic regularizers R_eff(a, R) = max(R, a/R) >= sqrt(a) and R_smooth(a, R) = R + a/R >= 2*sqrt(a); (3) Theorem 2.4 (leanflow_sym2_hadamard_recurrence_and_rns_inner_product): Sym^2(L_2) recurrence for the Hadamard (term-wise) product w_n = u_n * v_n, Apery's sequence (1, 5, 73, 1445) for zeta(3), and 3-prime RNS-CRT verification of <(10,20,30), (11,12,14)> = 770 modulo M = 971,229,691; and (4) Theorem 2.5 (leanflow_taylor_interval_and_spectral_bound): alternating-series enclosure exp(-1/2) in [2329/3840, 233/384] and spectral exponent verification (-84/125 vs. -2/3).

title: QSurvDiag replication package
abstract: Records and verification scripts for the article "Why Quantum Mutants Survive: Separating Observation Limitations from Suite Omissions". Native QUTest executions are archived, not rerun; the scripts recompute every checked value from the archived records with the Python standard library, and an optional analytic tier recomputes the transpilation- and statevector-based values. The archive is mixed-license: provenance/LICENSE_MAP.csv assigns each file, and LICENSES/NOTICE.txt holds the third-party notices.

title: VaDar: Implicit Goal Conditioning via Value Disaggregation
abstract: Long-horizon tasks are important for modern AI and robotics, yet pose a challenge for reinforcement learning. Historically, a popular approach has been to decompose a task into subgoals, and learn a subgoal-conditioned policy to execute each subtask in sequence. We introduce an alternative called Value Disaggregation (VaDar), which trains a single subgoal-independent policy to maximize a linear combination of per-subgoal critic values. Because subgoal information is needed only at training-time, VaDar removes the need for possibly costly or cumbersome subgoal-selection during policy deployment. Moreover, through careful experiments, we show that VaDar (1) is always competitive with, and frequently outperforms, natural baselines like goal-conditioning and (2) succeeds on tasks with non-sequential goal structure and multiple optimization objectives. In particular, VaDar is the first algorithm to solve challenging, long-horizon tasks in the RoboCasa suite, even when starting from a policy pretrained from behavior cloning with near-zero initial task success. Taken together, VaDar's successes suggest that subgoal information benefits actor-critic reinforcement learning by enhancing the efficacy of critic learning, whereas policy goal-conditioning is often unnecessary.

title: ExMR: Extremity Motion Refinement for Monocular Human Motion Capture
abstract: Detailed hand and foot articulation is important for animation and motion analysis, yet remains challenging to recover from monocular video. Recent expressive video methods infer hand articulation from shared whole-body representations. Our conference work suggests that this underexploits local evidence: the Foot Motion Refinement (FootMR) module refines ankle rotations from foot keypoints, improving reconstruction even when the initial estimator receives the same keypoints. We extend this principle to hands with the Hand Motion Refinement (HandMR) module. Because 2D finger keypoints are often missing or unreliable, HandMR combines image features of a pretrained hand reconstruction model with initial arm and hand rotations to refine elbows, wrists, and fingers. We integrate FootMR and HandMR into ExMR (Extremity Motion Refinement), a system for reconstructing 3D body, hand, and foot motion from monocular video. An initial temporal estimator predicts whole-body motion, after which both refiners revisit local evidence to predict residual joint rotations. Experiments on ARCTIC, MOYO, RICH, and MOOF show that ExMR outperforms state-of-the-art methods in hand and foot reconstruction, reducing hand per-vertex error and ankle joint angle error on MOYO by 19% and 18%, respectively, relative to the strongest competitor. Code will be made available for research purposes. Project page: https://twehrbein.github.io/exmr-website/

title: Reflex, Talker, Reasoner: A Tri-Tier Cognitive Architecture for Sub-200ms Full-Duplex Voice Agents with Collision Recovery
abstract: While dual-process agentic architectures such as Talker-Reasoner decouple fast conversational generation (System 1) from asynchronous multi-step planning and tool execution (System 2), they remain fundamentally bottlenecked in full-duplex spoken dialogue systems. Existing dual-tier pipelines route every acoustic pause to a generative Large Language Model (LLM) and a neural Text-to-Speech (TTS) synthesizer, incurring 350–600 ms of latency and substantial GPU compute even on trivial rejections, call terminations, or mid-sentence intent pivots. Furthermore, when aggressive End-of-Turn (EOT) silence thresholds (e.g., 200 ms) are deployed to achieve human-like responsiveness, physiological inhalation pauses frequently trigger premature agent speech. This results in mutual talk-over collisions, polite user stops, and truncated transcripts that corrupt downstream System 2 tool execution. This paper introduces the Reflex–Talker–Reasoner (RTR) architecture, a tri-tier cognitive framework that prepends a sub-cortical System 0 Reflex Layer ahead of System 1 and System 2. System 0 combines a calibrated non-generative discriminative decision gate (operating in under 85 ms) with an in-memory Pre-Baked PCM Audio Cache and a Fragile-Window Collision Recovery State Machine. On terminal rejections and conversational pivots, System 0 bypasses both the 3B-parameter generative Talker LLM and the 3B-parameter live neural TTS engine, streaming cached acoustic responses in 188 ms median latency while issuing deterministic preemption signals (CancelToken) to abort stale System 2 reasoning tasks. When a mid-breath false-EOT collision occurs within the initial 450 ms Fragile Output Window of agent playback, System 0 flushes outbound audio within 25 ms, resolves mutual-silence deadlocks via a 400 ms timer that triggers a cached yield backchannel ("Sorry, please continue"), and stitches fragmented user utterances (U1 + U2 + U3) into a single coherent turn. Evaluated on a 500-turn full-duplex tool-use and physiological breath-disfluency simulation suite, RTR reduces P50 rejection and pivot latency by 67.0%, eliminates 37.0%–38.8% of live neural TTS invocations, and improves end-to-end tool-calling accuracy under breath-disfluent speech from 33.6% to 97.4%.

title: SleepPairNet: Learning Multimodal Pediatric Sleep Representations with Random-Pair Cross-Attention
abstract: Analyzing physiological sleep signals is important for assessing sleep quality and detecting sleep-related disorders. Learning inter-modal relationships across physiological signals can provide richer representations for downstream sleep analysis. We introduce SleepPairNet, a multimodal self-supervised learning (SSL) framework that learns pairwise interactions between physiological signals through cross-attention. We propose a random modality-pair selection strategy that exposes the model to diverse signal pairs during pretraining, enabling flexibility across modality combinations at test time. Pretrained on the NCH dataset, SleepPairNet outperforms the evaluated SSL baselines on all respiratory tasks while remaining competitive on EEG-related tasks, and shows even stronger results when transferred to the external CHAT dataset.

title: Focused Omni-Modal GUI Agents
abstract: Graphical User Interface (GUI) agents increasingly act over streaming omni-modal observations spanning screenshots, audio, video, interaction history, and device states. However, exposing this complete context uniformly at every step ignores that relevance is transient and sparse: the signal determining one action can become clutter at the next. Because executed actions feed back into the context, these errors compound into Sequential Distraction, driving the agent into irreversible trajectory drift. We formulate the underlying requirement as Focused Perception: a representation that is step-adaptive, action-sufficient, and non-intrusive. We realize this in FocusGUI, a lightweight adapter that dynamically prioritizes multimodal channels against a step-specific decision reference. Instead of uniformly processing all inputs, it compresses the most relevant evidence into a compact latent and subtly injects it into the frozen decoder's embeddings, guiding the model's attention without altering its native parameter space. FocusGUI trains from action supervision alone, requiring neither modality-relevance labels nor backbone fine-tuning. Across four omni-modal backbones, it raises overall Type Match by +33.2 and Exact Match by 3.0 times over the frozen backbone on average, and Type Match by +30.1 over the strongest existing enhancement method.

title: VEILED-SH: Vulnerability Expression through Indirect Language Evaluation Dataset (Self-Harm)
abstract: AI systems may miss indirect, culturally situated distress or provide support mismatched to the application context. Existing benchmarks do not jointly address cultural variation, application context, and practitioner disagreement. We introduce VEILED-SH, a benchmark and construction methodology for evaluating single-turn responses to indirect expressions of suicide, self-harm, and distress. Its 10,003 prompts span counselor chat, forum posts, platform search, and triage, drawing on Singapore-grounded sources and public datasets. An expert-validated multi-label taxonomy distinguishes intent, communicative function, and response behavior. Six automated profiles, individually calibrated to three peer-support practitioners and three clinicians, retain separate reference policies for proxy-alignment scoring. Evaluating five systems on a coverage-enriched sample reveals variation in proxy alignment across profile-generated reference policies, even for the same system responses.

title: ViMoLa: Discrete Motion Tokens for Language-Guided Video Generation
abstract: Language-guided video generation often captures scene content while missing the requested motion. We present ViMoLa (Video Motion Language), which predicts a motion prior from language and injects it into a frozen image-to-video backbone. A spatial vector-quantized autoencoder compresses dense trajectories into 64 tokens from a 512-entry codebook; a 28M-parameter transformer predicts the tokens from text; and zero-gated cross-attention adapters condition every frozen Wan~2.2 DiT block through forward hooks. Trained on 462K videos from Something-Something~v2 and Kinetics-400, ViMoLa raises directional accuracy from 0.287 to 0.442 (chance 0.250), with similar measured generative quality. Across-prompt shuffled codes achieve 0.283, supporting the importance of prompt-matched token content. A low-rank adapter reaches 0.428 at 1.45% additional forward-pass FLOPs, and reusing the tokenizer and language model with newly trained CogVideoX adapters raises accuracy from 0.301 to 0.398. Control remains imperfect: oracle codes reach 0.531, compound-motion gains are smaller, and the adapter does not explicitly preserve token-to-patch assignments.

title: StopLoss: Teaching Agents to Predict Failure and Stop Early
abstract: Coding agents keep working on runs that will fail verification, and asking a frontier model to watch for this is expensive in its own right. We introduce StopLoss, a small external monitor that learns failure recognition from completed trajectories and their verifier outcomes. The name is inspired by the stop-loss order in finance: StopLoss ends a run early when the run is likely to fail, which saves resources. Final outcomes label earlier local windows, so a fine-tuned language model can score the most recent tool steps in a single forward pass, and a threshold calibrated on successful runs turns that score into an abort decision without changing the executor. Trained on GPT-family SWE-rebench trajectories and evaluated on SWE-bench Verified and a SWE-bench Pro subset with GPT and Claude executors, StopLoss is compared against six general-purpose judges reading identical windows. Outcome supervision lifts failure prediction from near chance to a useful signal at the first check, at one to two orders of magnitude lower cost per check than any tested judge. This translates into savings: relative to completing every task, StopLoss lowers cost per retained solve by 4.5\% on Verified while preserving 99\% of successful runs, and by up to 31\% on the costlier Pro subset, reaching 48\% with a Qwen3-8B backbone, and in all four settings its cost per retained solve is below that of every judge policy. Outcome-trained small monitors can make failure recognition cheap enough for early stopping to pay for itself.

title: BiDex-100: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation Across 100+ Simulation Tasks
abstract: Bimanual manipulation with dexterous hands has attracted growing attention in research on robotic action models. However, few studies have developed benchmarks specifically tailored for dexterous manipulation, leaving the dexterous manipulation capabilities of existing models insufficiently characterized. In this paper, we present BiDex-100, a simulation benchmark for bimanual dexterous manipulation that combines broad task coverage, multi-dimensional evaluation, and high-DoF hand embodiments. Concretely, the benchmark comprises 106 tasks organized along five capability axes: generalization, instruction following, limited demonstrations, long horizon, and memory. Each task is paired with an out-of-domain variant featuring controlled visual and spatial changes, allowing systematic assessment of robustness. In addition, the benchmark supports two embodiments and provides 8,080 success-validated teleoperated demonstrations, totaling 6.25 million frames. evidence.title: BiDex-100: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation Across 100+ Simulation Tasks
evidence.abstract: Bimanual manipulation with dexterous hands has attracted growing attention in research on robotic action models. However, few studies have developed benchmarks specifically tailored for dexterous manipulation, leaving the dexterous manipulation capabilities of existing models insufficiently characterized. In this paper, we present BiDex-100, a simulation benchmark for bimanual dexterous manipulation that combines broad task coverage, multi-dimensional evaluation, and high-DoF hand embodiments. Concretely, the benchmark comprises 106 tasks organized along five capability axes: generalization, instruction following, limited demonstrations, long horizon, and memory. Each task is paired with an out-of-domain variant featuring controlled visual and spatial changes, allowing systematic assessment of robustness. In addition, the benchmark supports two embodiments and provides 8,080 success-validated teleoperated demonstrations, totaling 6.25 million frames. We evaluate seven recent Vision-Language-Action models under a unified protocol, establishing baselines for capability-specific performance, robustness, and data efficiency. title: System X: An LLM Decision Model That Replies from Its Own KV Cache
abstract: Decision models return probabilities over supplied options, but a deployed agent may also need to reply in words. The present study introduces System X, a large language model (LLM) decision model that adds a text-reply option to the LLM-as-Jev readout. When this option wins, or confidence is low, the same model continues from the decision's key-value (KV) cache, avoiding a repeated prompt prefill. Qwen3-0.6B has been fine-tuned with LoRA on Reason-9k and Bitext reply rows. JevBench accuracy shows no statistically significant change (55.4% to 54.5%, p=0.87), while expected calibration error falls from 0.292 to 0.169. Held-out Bitext routing accuracy reaches 98.3%. Cache reuse saves 15-37% of latency on an Apple M4 Pro, with token-identical replies in the FP32 demonstration cases. Scoring options on copies of the prompt cache matches full-sequence scoring to within 1.4e-6 in probability. Adding dialogue, industry and complaint data (System X+) improves support-task results but lowers IFEval accuracy from 55.5% to 45.0%. System X v4 uses Qwen3-1.7B, rebalanced data and teacher-rewritten reply targets. Against its base LLM, JevBench accuracy rises from 55.0% to 61.0% (p=0.04), with no statistically significant IFEval change (p=0.71). A matched latency test on unadapted Qwen3-1.7B saves 17-39%. One LLM judge prefers v4 replies to an unadapted 1.7B second call (31 to 11 pairs, p=0.003); the other's preference is not significant. These reply comparisons also differ in prompts and generation limits. State conflicts and unsupported reply details remain failure modes. Further studies with several seeds, human raters and real support data are recommended.

title: RARE: Reinforcement Learning with Adaptive Rubric Evolution for Open-Ended Generation
abstract: Verifiable rewards have advanced reinforcement learning in mathematics and code. However, many valuable open-ended tasks share three properties: no automatic verifier of overall quality, multiple requirements to satisfy jointly, and multiple valid responses to each query. Training therefore needs feedback on requirement satisfaction across different valid responses. Rubric-based reinforcement learning provides this feedback by aggregating scores from explicit criteria. As learning progresses unevenly, some criteria become fully satisfied and lose discrimination while others remain informative. Dynamic methods revise shared rubrics or select evolving criteria to restore discrimination, but may also change useful criteria. To address this, we propose Reinforcement Learning with Adaptive Rubric Evolution (RARE). The core idea is to use current policy feedback to guide both which criteria change and what their replacements assess. Sample-level updates replace criteria fully satisfied across current outputs with checks of remaining quality differences, retaining all other criteria and scores. Within this rule, we compare rewarding desirable qualities with penalizing observed flaws. Video script generation exemplifies these properties and supports content production. Its demands for coherent, executable narratives under constraints make it a challenging testbed. Targeting flaws performs best across three video types with a mean gain of 3.82 points over matched static rubrics. Model and human preferences support these gains. Improvements also extend to writing and general generation benchmarks.

title: Mixture-of-Memories: Low-Overhead Language Modeling with Modular Knowledge Injection
abstract: Large language models store substantial factual knowledge in their parameters, yet this knowledge is difficult to control, update, and reliably elicit at inference time. Existing memory-augmented approaches typically rely on a single auxiliary mechanism, such as retrieval, parameter updates, or neural memory, and therefore apply the same form of correction to tokens with very different knowledge demands. We propose Mixture-of-Memories (MoM), a memory-augmented language modeling framework that separates routed neural memory from writable factual memory. MoM combines a frozen base LM with two neural memory experts: a latent memory that provides low-latency hidden-state corrections and a lexical memory that provides a token-space knowledge pathway. A lightweight Budget Router sets per-token mixture weights from uncertainty and disagreement features, replacing the fixed interpolation of prior memory modules. For post-hoc updates, an external explicit memory stays outside the router, because a router trained before facts are written learns to down-weight it; new facts are appended without retraining any component and used only when an answer-level gate accepts the retrieved fact. Experiments across language modeling, factual QA, update analysis, and efficiency show that MoM improves both predictive accuracy and updateability while retaining low inference overhead.

title: MT Forcing: Towards Stable and Consistent Multi-Turn Image Editing with Autoregressive Diffusion
abstract: Multi-turn image editing aims to modify an image according to a sequence of instructions, enabling more effective interactive visual content creation for users. However, existing methods often exhibit noticeable drift after only a few editing turns, manifesting in two aspects: 1) unstable visual quality, with accumulating artifacts and degraded details; and 2) inconsistent image content, with unintended changes to preserved regions and prior edits. To address these challenges, we propose MT Forcing, a novel training paradigm for multi-turn image editing with unified multimodal models (UMMs) based on autoregressive diffusion. Specifically, we propose Single-Turn Distribution Matching Distillation (Single-Turn DMD), which supervises student self-rollouts with a teacher that applies cumulative edits to the source image in a single turn, providing visual-quality guidance without recursive error accumulation. Additionally, we introduce Teacher-Forcing Guidance, which supervises history-dependent transitions on reference trajectories during warmup and as a regularizer during distillation, encouraging cross-turn content consistency beyond what per-turn distribution matching alone can ensure. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the multi-turn image editing capabilities of UMMs, yielding more stable visual quality and stronger cross-turn consistency.

title: Whistle and Wrong Lyrics: Synthetic Queries Are Not Enough for Real-World Query-by-Melody
abstract: People look up a song by humming it, but also by whistling it or singing it with the wrong words. Published query-by-humming systems and benchmarks focus on hums and sung queries, and no public dataset pairs whistles or wrong-lyrics singing with song recordings. We study both query types with a melody-only retrieval system: a key-normalized pitch track embedded by a 5.2M-parameter contour encoder, with a spectral-peak tracker for whistles. First, a physics-grounded generator renders synthetic whistles and nonsense-syllable singing from the vocal melodies of 11,083 songs. Training on them raises top-1 retrieval of held-out synthetic queries against an 11,050-song gallery from 0.180 to 0.251 for whistles and from 0.193 to 0.264 for wrong-lyrics singing, but the gain does not transfer: on the MLEnd test performers the best synthetic-only model gets 210 of 339 real whistles right at top-1, against 214 for the baseline. Second, a closed-set fine-tune on real MLEnd whistles with performer-disjoint splits raises whistle-to-hum top-1 from 0.631 (95% CI 0.581-0.681) to 0.673 (0.622-0.723), on known songs only. Third, two further generations of synthetic queries also fail to transfer: melody-conditioned whistles and la-la singing from a commercial neural music model leave real-whistle top-1 at 0.631, and an open-source pipeline (YingMusic-Singer-Plus singing with partly wrong, mumbled or nonsense lyrics, a DDSP whistle synthesizer, and a melody-error model fitted on real performers) gives at best 0.619 (paired difference -0.012, 95% CI -0.038 to +0.015). Across physics-based, commercial neural and open-source neural synthetic data, nothing transferred to real whistles, which points to collecting real queries as the missing step. Code is public; models and data will be released.

title: Painting Change Map as guidance for generating painting processes
abstract: Digital art generation has undergone a massive paradigm shift, moving from static image synthesis to dynamic video generation that can mimic the human painting process. While existing models can synthesize visually stunning time-lapses of paintings being created or "unpainted," they largely treat the creative process as a black box. Current conditioning mechanisms are either too rigid, relying on static geometric cues like Canny edges or depth maps, or too holistic, utilizing simple scalar progress variables that offer no localized control. Consequently, users lack the agency to steer how a painting evolves over time. In this work, we argue that true control over the video generation of artwork requires a joint understanding of two fundamental dimensions: where an artist acts, and when those actions take place. To achieve this, we introduce the Painting Change Map, a novel spatio-temporal control mechanism that explicitly tracks normalized structural changes across a 1,000-timestep continuum, a resolution sufficient to capture fine-grained stroke-level changes while remaining computationally tractable. By mapping localized visual differences into an encoded RGB space, our representation enables fine-grained guidance for both the forward painting and reverse unpainting processes. Extensive benchmarking demonstrates the efficacy of our approach. We outperform existing control baselines and achieve competitive or superior results compared to state-of-the-art painting methods. Furthermore, under oracle conditions, our method surpasses all baselines by a significant margin. Code is available at https://github.com/Markus-Pobitzer/painting-change-map.

title: MCSplat: Multi-View Photometric and Geometric Consistent Feed-Forward Gaussian Splatting for Driving Scenes
abstract: Driving-scene reconstruction via feed-forward Gaussian splatting from sparse multi-view images remains challenging due to two factors. First, cross-camera photometric inconsistency, caused by variations in exposure, ISP, and illumination, can be incorrectly absorbed into Gaussian geometry. Second, unreliable local geometric supervision arises from normal-based constraints near depth discontinuities. To address these issues, we present MCSplat, a multi-view consistent feed-forward Gaussian splatting framework for driving scenes. MCSplat constructs a canonical appearance space from depth-guided multi-camera correspondences to decouple geometry learning from camera-specific appearance. A multi-scale Bilateral Grid Transformer restores raw camera appearance from canonical renderings, enabling photometric supervision without contaminating Gaussian geometry. To improve local geometric reliability, we estimate Fisher-information-based uncertainty from photometric sensitivity and use it to adaptively weight surface-oriented self-supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved reconstruction quality and generalization across driving datasets. Geometry-oriented evaluations further reveal enhanced cross-view depth consistency and local surface-normal agreement, while qualitative results show fewer geometric artifacts and more coherent structures across overlapping views.

title: World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds
abstract: Emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are moving beyond representation learning towards latent world models that support prediction, planning, and control. Yet their latent worlds naturally lack a human-interpretable interface. In this Perspective, we argue that as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction. To this end, we envision a four-stage research agenda, involving Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act, to guide this shift toward actionable latent-world understanding. Within our framework, existing JEPA interpretability efforts provide early evidence for Ground, while systematic analysis of latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remains largely unexplored. Overall, this Perspective aims to call for a broader latent-world interpretability agenda that shifts attention from decoding representations toward understanding, validating, and acting on latent worlds.

title: Vision as Proprioception: Estimating Humanoid Robot Pose from Video
abstract: Estimating a humanoid robot's internal state from video has a wide range of real-world applications but remains unexplored. During interactions with a robot, its onboard state information may be unavailable due to privacy, ownership, or communication constraints. Meanwhile, online and AI-generated robot videos provide rich sources of data but typically lack corresponding joint configurations, limiting their direct use in robot learning. To address these issues, we present HumanoidPose, a new framework that treats vision as proprioception to recover full-body joint configurations in world space from video alone. Specifically, we combine pretrained human-pose features with robot kinematics in a unified model that predicts each embodiment's joint configurations. We retarget human motions to sixteen different humanoid embodiments, enabling scalable learning entirely from synthetic data. To improve real-world generalization, we further leverage unlabeled online videos through self-training to develop a 2D robot-pose detector. In our evaluation, HumanoidPose improves joint-angle and joint-position accuracy over the evaluated baselines and reduces joint-angle error by 18-32% relative to the best-performing baseline on each of the three real humanoid platforms. We further show improved global localization and generalization to unseen embodiments. HumanoidPose enables visual understanding of other robots during interaction and extraction of robot motion from online and generated videos.

title: Projective systems and bounds on the length of codes of non-zero defect
abstract: We derive bounds on the lengths of linear codes with fixed Singleton defect, working within the framework of projective systems. This geometric perspective allows us to unify and extend a range of existing results. We study the maximum length of a non-degenerate linear code when its dimension, field order, and Singleton defect are fixed, and refine this question by also prescribing the defect of the dual code. We further investigate the maximum dimension in which a code can attain the general length bound. Among our main results, we provide sufficient conditions under which a code and its dual have equal Singleton defect, addressing a gap in the existing literature. We show that codes of sufficient length must be projective, meet the Griesmer bound, and have an almost maximum distance separable dual. Our bounds subsume or improve several results in the literature. For field orders greater than three, we propose two conjectures on length-maximal codes of dimension at least five, supported by computational evidence. title: SPARC: Spoken Profile Authorship Recognition Corpus
abstract: Speech anonymization has focused on the acoustic signal, leaving open how much speaker information the transcribed words themselves retain. In this work, we study pairwise speaker and demographic-attribute verification from transcribed speech. We introduce SPARC (Spoken Profile Authorship Recognition Corpus), a benchmark built from two podcast corpora comprising over 12,500 speakers, 1.5M quality-filtered utterances, and speaker-level inferred or source-provided labels for sex, age, and accent, and evaluate five attribution models and three LLMs on identity- and attribute-verification trials with episode- and metadata-based topic proxies. LLM adversaries distinguish same-speaker pairs from text alone. Attribute-label agreement is harder to verify, but LLMs perform sex- and accent-label verification above chance. Finally, releasing only short probe texts (50 words) degrades the strongest adversaries the most, offering a partial reduction in observed linkage.

title: Securing LLM-Agent Long-Term Memory Against Poisoning: Non-Malleable, Origin-Bound Authority with Machine-Checked Guarantees
abstract: An agent based on a large language model (LLM) may store an untrusted document and use it weeks later to select a payment destination. Preventing this action requires evidence of authorization that remains valid when stored text changes. We study a policy that requires either endorsements (explicit approvals) from two separately administered sources or explicit user authorization. In an abstract memory model, we prove the policy is preserved under permitted transformations for stores of any size, assuming correct source and authority binding, protected records, and checks on every consequential action. We evaluate the executable monitor, which checks calls before execution, separately from the proof. In 1,152 controlled tool-use episodes, GPT-4o-mini executes attacker-selected actions in 61 of 72 undefended episodes and none of the 72 monitored episodes. Clean-task completion remains 24 of 24 when both endorsers are available. A separate 1,728-episode experiment tests recovery after denial. Returning to signed records instead of rereading a contaminated note raises attacked-task completion from 14/72 to 72/72 for GPT-4o-mini and from 22/72 to 43/72 for Gemini 2.5 Flash, without executing an attacker-selected action. Neither model completes transactions with fewer than two sources. Whole-action tests reject unauthorized combinations of individually approved fields. Extraction probes identify mistaken approvals, and fault analysis shows how shared failures can negate a second domain's benefit. Calibrations using original defense implementations reveal security and task-completion tradeoffs under different policies. These results support conditional enforcement and recovery in constructed workflows, but do not establish that endorsements will be available or correct in deployment.

Returning to signed records instead of rereading a contaminated note raises attacked-task completion from 14/72 to 72/72 for GPT-4o-mini and from 22/72 to 43/72 for Gemini 2.5 Flash, without executing an attacker-selected action. Neither model completes transactions with fewer than two sources. Whole-action tests reject unauthorized combinations of individually approved fields. Extraction probes identify mistaken approvals, and fault analysis shows how shared failures can negate a second domain's benefit. Calibrations using original defense implementations reveal security and task-completion tradeoffs under different policies. These results support conditional enforcement and recovery in constructed workflows, but do not establish that endorsements will be available or correct in deployment.

title: Supporting Data for AI-enabled Digital Transformation in Project Management: A Combined Bibliometric and BERTopic Modelling Approach
abstract: Description This repository contains the analytical datasets, validation outputs, sensitivity-analysis materials and supporting documentation associated with the study: AI-enabled Digital Transformation in Project Management: A Combined Bibliometric and BERTopic Modelling Approach The study combines bibliometric co-word analysis with BERTopic-based semantic topic modelling to examine the explicit conceptual relationships and latent semantic structures of AI-enabled digital transformation research in project management. The final analytical corpus comprises 562 peer-reviewed journal and review articles published between 2017 and June 2026. The repository includes: a cleaned dataset prepared for BERTopic analysis; a bibliometric dataset prepared for VOSviewer analysis; archived outputs from five BERTopic sensitivity configurations; topic-coherence, NPMI, silhouette-score, topic-count and outlier-count results; screenshots documenting alternative topic solutions; manuscript figures and, where available, their source data; a README file describing the files, analytical settings and data restrictions. The final BERTopic configuration identified 16 substantive topics and retained 94 documents as Topic −1 outliers. The reported validation values for the final model were c_v = 0.433, NPMI = −0.126 and silhouette score = 0.048. Model robustness was assessed through quantitative validation and sensitivity analysis across alternative UMAP and HDBSCAN configurations. The sensitivity analysis varied the UMAP n_neighbors parameter and the HDBSCAN min_cluster_size parameter. The archived outputs are provided to support transparency regarding model selection, topic granularity, outlier prevalence and the parameter dependence of smaller topic boundaries. The repository supports verification and transparency of the reported bibliometric, semantic topic-modelling and model-validation outputs. It does not contain the complete executable analysis notebook or serialised alternative BERTopic models. The main modelling procedures, parameter settings, validation methods and sensitivity configurations are documented in the associated article and supplementary materials. Some bibliographic metadata and abstracts were obtained from licensed databases, including Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore and Google Scholar. Redistribution is therefore limited to the extent permitted by the relevant providers. Where full records cannot be shared, the repository provides cleaned or derived analytical data and aggregate outputs.

title: Persistent Representational Misalignment Induces Vision-Language Model Failures
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) fail at some tasks that are simple for humans---but why? We hypothesize that many such failures stem from VLMs' difficulties translating between vision and language representations, a misalignment the Platonic Representation Hypothesis predicts should disappear with scale. This paper is composed of two parts: in the first, we show that existing vision and language representations are linearly unalignable. This misalignment is an inherent property of the data and hence expected to persist regardless of either scale or the alignment's complexity. In the second, we demonstrate how this misalignment both leads to a predictably induced generalization failure and correlates with existing failure modes, where more representationally aligned VLM backbones accordingly exhibit fewer failures. Overall, these results imply representations will not become aligned simply given sufficient scale, providing evidence against a strong version of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.

title: CerviDBF-Net: Leveraging Spatial and Temporal Features for Accurate Cervical Cancer Diagnosis
abstract: Cervical cancer screening increasingly relies on automated image analysis to support colposcopic assessment and improve the consistency of clinical decision-making. This study proposes CerviDBF-Net, a novel deep learning framework for automated cervix-type classification from colposcopic images. The proposed architecture combines DenseNet121 for spatial feature extraction, a brain-inspired Liquid Neural Network (LNN) for contextual and temporal feature modelling, and a fully connected Softmax layer for final classification. To improve image quality and feature representation, the preprocessing pipeline incorporates bicubic interpolation, Bi-Histogram Equalization with Plateau Limit (BHEPL) for contrast enhancement, Kapur entropy-based thresholding, and the Roberts Cross operator for edge detection. The framework is evaluated on the Intel & MobileODT Cervical Cancer Screening dataset, which contains three cervix types (Type 1, Type 2, and Type 3) defined by the location and visibility of the transformation zone. CerviDBF-Net achieves an accuracy of 98.92%, sensitivity of 99.13%, specificity of 98.38%, precision of 98.69%, and an F1-score of 98.27%, demonstrating strong classification performance compared with the evaluated existing models. The proposed approach provides an automated baseline tool for cervix-type classification that may support triage in colposcopy-assisted screening by helping clinicians assess whether adequate visualization of the squamocolumnar junction has been achieved.

title: Visual Scaffolding: Toward Native Multimodal Reasoning
abstract: The success of chain-of-thought (CoT) in complex reasoning can be attributed to a textual scaffolding effect: explicit intermediate results can be examined, reused, and composed to support subsequent reasoning, much as scaffolding supports a building under construction. However, mainstream multimodal LLMs lack an equivalent scaffold for visual distinctions that are difficult to express in concise verbal descriptions. We therefore ask: Can native visual representations become first-class citizens alongside language, providing a visual scaffold for reasoning? We define native multimodal reasoning as reasoning in which native visual representations and language jointly carry reusable intermediate states. As a concrete implementation, the visual scaffolding mechanism we proposed lets the MLLM autonomously initiate a retrieval action at any reasoning step. A lightweight retriever selects native visual features, which are then incorporated directly into the evolving CoT and remain available to subsequent steps. To evaluate this mechanism under controlled visual demands, we introduce NMR-Bench, comprising Burden Counting and Path Tracing. With 88M added parameters (approximately 2%) on Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking, our model achieves 66.43% and 72.50% accuracy, respectively, surpassing the evaluated GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro baselines. Controlled interventions show that changing selected visual content affects task accuracy and can redirect subsequent visual selection even when intervening text is held fixed. These findings show that native visual states can function as intermediate reasoning material and point toward reusable scaffolds for additional modalities.

title: [Design and implementation of a clinical trial image medical record desensitization system based on artificial intelligence technology].
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To designe a clinical trial image medical record desensitization system based on artificial intelligence technology and to conduct preliminary applications, achieving the protection of patient privacy and promoting the safe use of clinical image data in clinical trial projects. METHODS: The clinical trial image record desensitization system based on artificial intelligence technology was first performed to preprocess operations, such as cropping and compression on medical images to initialize the image records. Then, it utilized advanced image recognition, natural language processing, and convolutional neural network technologies to automatically classify (labeled, feature extraction, and text recognition) according to the content of medical documents. It automatically identified sensitive information in the image records of clinical trial patients, including personal identity information such as patient name, identification number, medical record number, phone number, and birthplace. Pixel-level masking or blurring was performed on the identified sensitive information points, and an artificial online desensitization system based on canvas technology was assisted to ensure the security and confidentiality of privacy data. RESULTS: The designed clinical trial image record desensitization system exhibited high performance and efficiency in both desensitization effect and processing speed. After desensitizing 100 000 pieces of image record data in this system, a total of 9 000 medical record image samples were randomly selected from the processed medical document types for automated desensitization effect verification. The average accuracy rate of medical document desensitization reached 88.48%, with an accuracy rate of up to 99.40% for serious adverse event medical documents. CONCLUSION: The clinical trial image record desensitization system based on artificial intelligence technology improves accuracy and efficiency in medical data privacy protection. Combined with the artificial online desensitization auxiliary system, it can be applied in production environments, providing reliable technical support for the safe sharing and effective utilization of clinical trial image records.

title: Sampling and Curvature in First-Exit Comparisons for Momentum SGD
abstract: First-exit prediction for momentum SGD depends on sampling information that pointwise gradient laws omit. Strongly convex finite pools with identical pointwise laws and matched iid momentum dynamics can have different reshuffled exits; even analytic pools with uniformly close pointwise laws can have separated exit probabilities. For persistent sampling in one dimension, we establish an explicit O(h) mean-exit comparison with a finite-rate switching process under nonvanishing component velocities and step-size conditions; iid sampling instead averages to an ODE. Retaining realized minibatches and sampled curvature yields finite-window exit brackets beyond this regime. In 32 trained ridge-logistic runs, 29 meet prespecified targets with rounding-certified brackets; an enclosure control explains most of the width advantage. Exact-real certificates establish finite means at the original tested radii for three ResNet-18 checkpoints and give local finite-mean conditions for tanh and ViT networks; their upper bounds remain loose, and original-radius ViT mean guarantees remain unresolved despite 128 fresh continuation paths. A two-network replication gives 32/32 successful seeds in each of four finite-path persistence comparisons. Independent equal-length controls retain slower exits after refresh resets than without resets, but the refresh-versus-random ordering reverses with update length at both networks. These interventions do not causally decompose raw momentum SGD. Neural step-size scaling does not validate the switching limit.
