title: A Secure and Transparent Approach to Internet Voting: Validating End-to-End Verification in Digital Election Process
abstract: Internet voting methods make voting easier, more accessible, and more inclusive in contemporary democracies. It also raises privacy, security, and manipulation concerns. Emphasizing the need of E2E verification, this paper addresses secure and open online voting. We provide a paradigm to safeguard voter anonymity and vote integrity using homomorphic encryption, blockchain, and digital signatures among prominent cryptographic techniques. Voters and election authorities may examine and monitor every vote using our open, auditable system without compromising anonymity. By assuring open, verifiable, and tamper-proof voting systems, this solution tackles online voting system challenges and becomes ready for secure digital elections. The paper investigates scalability of the paradigm, practical uses, and adoption possibilities. Voter involvement and accessibility rise as internet voting is more common. Important problems, however, include integrity, security, and openness. For digital elections, this paper presents an open, safe online voting system with E2E confirmation. Modern cryptographic techniques maintain votes secret, undamaged, and verifiable without compromising voter anonymity by means of homomorphic encryption, digital signatures, and blockchain technology. Vote correctness, verification time, and attack resistance define the precision of the proposed system. Its fit for major elections is also assessed in terms of scalability, security, and efficiency. Thanks to extensive modeling and real-world case studies, the system has minimal latency, great vote accuracy, and strong security resilience. Results show that the proposed architecture surpasses standard election systems in performance and security. Blockchain transparency makes every vote auditable in real time, reassuring voters and authorities. This study finishes with a review of the system's potential for safe, scalable, and transparent digital elections to prepare for future deployments.

title: The Missing Compliance Class: LLM Graders That Collapse Jailbreak Success, and a Free Check
abstract: Jailbreak papers report an attack success rate, the share of responses that deliver the harmful request, and read it as a property of the target model. We hold the target model, the prompts and the responses fixed and change only the grader. Three dense graders of 8B and 9B parameters, from three model families, move compliant responses to the neighbouring class, evasion, instead of scattering them across classes. One of them assigns the compliance label zero times in 900 responses. This class collapse also appears on new harmful requests, on a target model from a third family, and in a held-out 7B grader from a fourth family. Per-class label counts expose it at no cost and without human labels. The collapse decides how the rate behaves under a change of grader. On two corpora of 900 responses and eight graders, the compliance rate differs by a factor of 22 to 25, while the non-refusal rate differs by 18 to 23 percentage points. Without the three collapsing graders, compliance differs by a factor of 1.7 to 2.8 on all four corpora, and non-refusal still differs by 10 to 22 points. These results do not change when every grader is called once. We propose a reporting minimum that keeps the compliance rate and adds its per-class label counts and the named grader. Beside it goes the non-refusal rate, whose disagreement across graders is additive.

title: A Revocable Certificateless Aggregate Signature Scheme with Efficient Invalid Signature Detection for Next Generation Vehicular Networks
abstract: Next-Generation Vehicular Networks (NGVNs) rely on the continuous exchange of safety and traffic-related information among vehicles and roadside infrastructure. Ensuring the authenticity of these messages while maintaining low communication and computation overhead remains a critical challenge. Although certificateless aggregate signature schemes provide an effective solution by eliminating certificate management and reducing verification costs, most existing approaches offer limited support for identifying invalid signatures within aggregated messages and handling vehicle revocation efficiently. To address these issues, this paper presents a revocable certificateless aggregate signature (RCAS) scheme based on elliptic curve cryptography. The proposed scheme avoids expensive bilinear pairing operations, making it suitable for resource-constrained and latencysensitive vehicular environments. An efficient invalid signature identification mechanism is incorporated to locate malicious signatures within an aggregate signature through a divide-andconquer strategy, thereby reducing verification overhead. In addition, a lightweight revocation framework based on a cuckoo filter is introduced to enable fast detection and exclusion of compromised vehicles. The security of the proposed scheme is analyzed in the Random Oracle Model against both Type-I and Type-II adversaries. Furthermore, performance evaluation demonstrates that the scheme achieves lower computational and communication costs while supporting efficient revocation and invalid signature detection. These features make the proposed RCAS scheme a practical and scalable authentication solution for large-scale next-generation vehicular networks.

title: RIDI-REAL-UPDATES-v1.1: Individual correctness change after model updates — QA-corrected prospective fresh start
abstract: Preregistered technical-correction, whole-study fresh restart evaluating whether nondeclining aggregate benchmark scores conceal individual-question correctness changes in fixed public model-release pairs. Six pinned incumbent–successor pairs (12 exact model revisions) answer 800 frozen retrieved-reference questions (Natural Questions 250, HotpotQA 250, FEVER 300) in two fixed conditions (main one question, floor batches of 16): 24 wholly new scientific units. Three confirmatory hypotheses H1–H3, six secondary endpoints S1–S6, equal-benchmark weights, 100,000 joint benchmark-stratified paired bootstrap resamples (seed 20261013), technical-failure rules and archived code are frozen in the source project's attached corrected ZIP. Earlier V1 https://osf.io/ras42/ produced four terminal pair-1 units and one p3_incumbent floor KeyError-blocked attempt; all case-level V1 results remained unopened and none is reused. Four context metadata limits previously observed during tokenizer preflight were repaired. Prepublication QA added two disclosed implementation safeguards (non-vacuous H1 no-C0 status; strict V1.1 output root), BEFORE publication or V1.1 generation. The source questions, frozen predictors and earlier PREDICT/P8 findings pre-exist; no new V1.1 scientific answers exist. Some source data are restricted and identified by immutable SHA-256 provenance rather than redistributed. Local aggregate-score acceptance is a study rule, NOT evidence of provider adoption.

title: Bellman Language Models: Solving the Recurring Decisions of LLM Agents
abstract: A general observation in agentic workflows, especially bounded ones, is that the decision space of the LLM, when we separate a decision from generation, starts approaching saturation: the agent meets the same states again and again, and after enough conversations it stops meeting new ones. LLMs generally don't treat these decisions as an optimization problem and instead re-derive them from their context/prompt on every turn. We show that treating decision making within reasonable bounds as an optimization problem, solving it once, and reusing the solved decisions can often make an agent faster, cheaper and more reliable. Our approach, which we call Discretize, Then Decide, starts from data such as the workflow's own logs or, when none exists, runs of the LLM agent itself. It reads each conversation into discrete states and estimates the probability of each outcome and the cost of each move, until no new states appear and the probabilities stop changing. It then solves the resulting Markov decision process. The solution runs as a controller around the model, sending moves whose content is fixed in the state, such as a tool call or a templated reply, and any state it hasn't seen is sent back to the LLM. We call an LLM run this way a Bellman language model (BLM), after Richard Bellman's equation for the best move in each state. On $τ^2$-bench telecom, the controller with no model solves 79% of tasks. As a BLM, Qwen3.8-27B, an open model, goes from 29% to 96% with 93% fewer model calls. For Claude Opus 5.5, which solves 96% of tasks on its own, running it as a BLM cuts model calls and cost per task by about 98% and lets it solve 2 more tasks. On InventoryBench, the solved policy with no model beats every published method. Where the hard part is writing content rather than choosing moves, such as resolving SymPy issues, few decisions can be solved in advance, and a BLM helps little.

title: Good Judgment, Bad Advice: Decision-Model Controllers Raise Agent Cost Without Improving Success
abstract: Agent scaffolds increasingly delegate small decisions (whether to stop, verify, or change approach) to cheaper models. We ask whether a typed decision model, Jev 1.13, consulted only at deterministic decision points, makes a Claude Sonnet 5.5 terminal agent cheaper without making it worse. In a pre-specified study on Terminal-Bench 2.1, we hold one agent loop fixed and vary only the controller: none, deterministic rules, a small LLM (Claude Haiku 5.5) answering the same questions, Jev, and a placebo that samples Jev's development-phase choice frequencies at the same moments. On 21 held-out tasks (315 trials), Jev raised cost per attempt by 19% (geometric-mean ratio 1.19, 95% CI 1.02-1.36) at an identical pass rate (73.0% vs. 73.0%). Jev was cheaper than the small-LLM controller (ratio 0.81) but 22% more expensive than the placebo, and no pass-rate difference between arms was detectable. Offline, Jev ranked finish requests better than the alternatives (AUROC 0.78 vs. 0.62 for rules and 0.60 for the small LLM) but was poorly calibrated: its mean probability that a run was complete was 0.50 when 87% of those runs passed, so it asked the agent to verify work that was already correct. No controller ever chose to abandon a run. Informative decision signals did not become useful interventions; we discuss what that would require.

title: EdgeKernelBench: Unified LLM-Driven Kernel Generation for Edge Backends
abstract: Recent works show that LLMs can generate kernels with strong performance on server GPUs. Edge deployment presents distinct challenges because the hardware is heterogeneous, the software stacks are fragmented, and the resource budgets are tight. LLM kernel generation across diverse edge backends has yet to be studied systematically. We introduce EdgeKernelBench, which combines a unified IR deployment framework with a hierarchical benchmark for edge workloads. The unified IR captures reusable computation, scheduling, and memory decisions and connects to each target backend through a compiler interface. The benchmark spans progressively larger program scopes, from individual operators to compact model graphs, across representative edge application domains. We instantiate the design with TVM as a reference compiler and validate it across heterogeneous edge backends. With a single generation attempt, the best model achieves 64.5% Correct@1 but only 25.5% Fast@1.0. This gap shows that functional correctness does not consistently translate into performance gains. We therefore introduce the Layered Edge Kernel Agent (LEKA), which organizes optimization through a layered IR. On the agent evaluation subset, LEKA achieves 43.5% Fast@1.0, compared with 13.0% for direct generation and 26.1% for Claude Code. LEKA and Claude Code use the same base model and optimization budget. Together, EdgeKernelBench and LEKA support unified evaluation and layered optimization of kernels generated by LLMs across edge backends.

title: Testing Whether Anthropic and OpenAI Agents Solve PhD-Level Problems: Self-Generated, Code-Verified Multiple Choice Questions, Demonstrated on LEAN-Bench
abstract: Anthropic and OpenAI provide agents (Claude Code and Codex CLI) that write and run code until a task is done. We test the null hypothesis that these agents can solve PhD-level problems, stated as choosing the verified option on at least 90% of items, with a one-sided exact binomial test fixed before any evaluation attempt. The problems come from LEAN-Bench, a benchmark of LLM-written algorithmic trading code in which every strategy has 4 parts (a reason to buy, buy details, a reason to sell and sell details). The parts come from a library of 160 snippets, extended with option, risk, econometric and intraday analytics on real one-minute market data. The same model generates an open-ended question, writes the program that solves it and turns it into a multiple choice question. Its 4 wrong options are the executed outputs of mutants of that program (a wrong boundary, a wrong element, a skipped step, a wrong convention or a wrong order). An item is kept only if the same model without tools chooses a wrong option and the same model inside its vendor agent chooses the verified option. From 60 Anthropic and 60 OpenAI candidates, 52 items passed both gates. Claude Code with Claude Sonnet 5.5 chose the verified option on 52 of 52 items and Codex CLI with GPT-6.1 Sol on 52 of 52. We fail to reject the null hypothesis for both agents. Time and dollars to solution separate them where accuracy does not: 16 seconds and $0.070 per solved item for Claude Code and 35 seconds and $0.051 for Codex. A customized agent built around the mutation classes, LEAN-Bench Solver, matched their accuracy with GPT-6 Luna at $0.0029 per solved item. Without tools, the 4 models tested chose the verified option on between 9 of 52 and 17 of 52 accepted items (chance is 1 in 5). With tools, every multiple choice evaluation attempt was correct except those of LEAN-Bench Solver on DeepSeek V4 Flash (30 of 52). Generating an accepted item cost several times more than solving it. GPT-6.1 Sol without tools chose the verified option on 36 of 56 of its own candidates at the prior gate, which shows why that gate is needed. Every prompt, program, mutant, gate decision and attempt is provided with the paper.

title: Dual Task Vector Merging: Leveraging Emotion and ASR Knowledge for Low-Resource Alzheimer's Disease Detection
abstract: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) detection from speech benefits from both paralinguistic and linguistic cues, yet model training is frequently constrained by limited data. Fine-tuning a large pretrained speech encoder can easily overfit, while a frozen probe leaves the encoder's task-relevant knowledge underutilized. Therefore, we propose Dual Task Vector Merging, a parameter-efficient method that adapts a frozen wav2vec 2.0 backbone using task knowledge learned outside the AD task. Specifically, we inject two task vectors, derived as weight deltas from emotion- and ASR-fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0 models, into each transformer layer. During AD training, only layer-wise merging coefficients and a linear classification head are optimized, updating less than 0.1% of the parameters required for full fine-tuning. Speaker-independent experiments on ADReSS and ADReSSo show that dual merging improves over frozen probes, LoRA, and full fine-tuning, in the main binary settings, and gives the best results when combined with LoRA. Evaluation on PROCESS further shows that our advantages transfer to three-class HC/MCI/dementia classification when paired with LoRA. Experiments under reduced training data (20%, 40%, and 80%) confirm reliable gains in low-resource settings.

title: Modeling Uncertainty Propagation in 3D Morphable Models
abstract: We study the problem of mapping parameter-space variance of a 3D Morphable Model (3DMM) to per-vertex variance. Traditionally, per-vertex variance has been used to visually interpret the learnt parameter uncertainty. However, mapping parameter-space variance to per-vertex using sampling or error propagation is computationally expensive. We address this limitation with Closed-form Local Uncertainty Estimation (CLUE), which transforms the parameter-space distribution of 3DMMs to per-vertex through a closed-form approximation. CLUE emerges from applying the law of total variance to the 3DMM formulation and is modular, computationally inexpensive, and accurate. Subsequently, we study integrating CLUE for in-the-wild human mesh recovery training and inference. We note that CLUE uses the geometry of the mesh as an inductive bias when predicting the variance, leading to improved accuracy. Through extensive qualitative and quantitative experiments, we show that when used in training, CLUE (1) outpeforms probabilistic and deterministic baselines on metrics evaluating joints, mesh and uncertainty, and (2) has the highest uncertainty-to-error spearman correlation, with applications including data mining and interpretable uncertainty. Finally, we share SAM 3D Body (CLUE) which augments the regressor with high resolution uncertainty maps. We make our code available at https://github.com/vita-epfl/CLUE

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Evidence and Mutual-Evidence Mechanisms in Multiple Large Language Models: A Unified Framework for Dynamic Evidence Coordination
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generate answers using learned representations and contextual information, but their outputs may contain unsupported claims, inaccurate statements, incomplete reasoning, and inconsistencies with available sources. Evidence-based processing can help identify and reduce these problems through evidence retrieval, claim verification, source evaluation, and contradiction analysis. These operations can be conducted within an individual model's processing workflow or through interactions among multiple models. However, neither individual evidence assessment nor unconditional multi-model evidence coordination is necessarily optimal for every task. Individual assessment may preserve computational efficiency but overlook unsupported assumptions, whereas cross-model evidence assessment may introduce redundant judgments, correlated errors, communication overhead, and false consensus. This paper proposes Adaptive Switching between Self-Evidence and Mutual-Evidence Mechanisms (ASSM-ME), a conceptual framework for dynamically selecting and combining individual-model and cross-model evidence-processing mechanisms. Self-evidence mechanisms enable an individual model to identify claims, retrieve or inspect available evidence, evaluate source relevance, detect unsupported statements, and revise its output. Mutual-evidence mechanisms enable multiple models to independently assess evidence, exchange source assessments, compare claim-level judgments, identify contradictions, and coordinate evidence-based revisions. A state-aware controller considers evidence sufficiency, source reliability, claim importance, model disagreement, evidence independence, residual uncertainty, historical mechanism effectiveness, and computational cost when selecting the next mechanism. The framework supports transitions among individual evidence assessment, collaborative evidence analysis, cross-model verification, evidence-guided correction, and evidence-based termination. A cost-sensitive decision objective, reference algorithm, implementation architecture, research hypotheses, and experimental evaluation protocol are presented. The framework is a proposed research design rather than an empirically validated system. Its potential contribution is the formulation of evidence-mechanism selection as a sequential control problem spanning heterogeneous individual and collaborative evidence operations. Its novelty and practical value require comparison with existing fact-verification, retrieval-augmented generation, and adaptive multi-agent methods, followed by controlled empirical evaluation.

title: Founding Adaptive Computational Science: A New Discipline for the General Theory, Design, and Evolution of Adaptive Computation
abstract: Adaptive computational mechanisms have emerged across numerical simulation, artificial intelligence, optimization, control, scientific modeling, and distributed computing. However, the existence of adaptive algorithms and adaptive computational systems does not, by itself, establish a unified scientific discipline devoted to understanding adaptation as a general property of computation. This paper proposes Adaptive Computational Science (ACS) as a distinct interdisciplinary research discipline concerned with the principles, mathematical foundations, design methods, and empirical laws governing how computational systems determine when, why, and how their computational mechanisms should change. The central proposition of ACS is that adaptation should be studied not only as a technique for improving a particular algorithm, but also as a general computational phenomenon involving changes in representation, procedures, objectives, internal organization, interactions, resource allocation, and governing rules. The paper distinguishes Adaptive Computational Science as a proposed scientific discipline from adaptive computation as a class of computational processes and techniques. It introduces a general formal model of adaptive computation, identifies seven principal dimensions of adaptation, proposes a layered theoretical architecture, and formulates foundational research propositions concerning adaptation value, switching costs, structural change, stability, transferability, and verifiability. It further establishes a research methodology based on controlled comparisons, formal analysis, cross-domain replication, and standardized evaluation. Rather than claiming that all component ideas are unprecedented, this paper defines a research program through which their relationships can be investigated within a common conceptual and mathematical framework. Its long-term objective is to determine whether generalizable laws of computational adaptation can be established across otherwise different computational domains.

title: Campus public opinion monitoring method based on Bi-LSTM and attention mechanism
abstract: With the widespread use of social media on campus, online public opinion has become a major factor affecting the stability of universities. Traditional public opinion monitoring methods mainly rely on keyword filtering and statistical models. These methods fail to capture the contextual semantic features of text and lack the ability to predict the dynamic evolution of sudden opinion events. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a campus online public opinion monitoring model that combines Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory and Attention Mechanism. The Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory learns the temporal features of text in both directions, enhancing its ability to represent contextual information. The Attention Mechanism dynamically focuses on key opinion-related words, improving the efficiency of extracting critical information. Experimental results show that the model achieved an F1 score of 0.81 and a recall of 0.72 on the THUCNews dataset, slightly lower than BERT’s 0.73. On the Twitter dataset, the recall was 0.75. In sentiment analysis, the model achieved a strength score of 0.82 on 10,000 data points, 0.07 higher than the second-best model. In terms of text analysis efficiency, the proposed model achieves 78.35% on the THUCNews dataset and 82.47% on the Twitter dataset, both higher than the three comparative models. These results demonstrate that the proposed model has high accuracy and applicability in sentiment classification of campus public opinion. It provides a new approach for public opinion monitoring on campus and supports its development toward efficient systems.

title: SpriteStage: Long Horizon Animation Generation via Progressive Scene Programming and Replay
abstract: Video generation models synthesize visual sequences from text and image inputs. Extending video generation to long animations requires actions, dialogue, camera coverage, and narrative developments to remain coordinated across scenes. Executable scene programs make these decisions available for inspection. Constructing an entire story before observing its execution can leave later scenes dependent on unrealized events. We present SpriteStage, a progressive scene programming framework that builds animation through iterative enactment and engine reorchestration. Iterative enactment generates each scene from an accepted world checkpoint and narrative snapshot, executes it on a shared spatial stage, and uses runtime and visual feedback to revise the relevant actions or story beats. The accepted outcome becomes the starting state for the next scene. Engine reorchestration maps the resulting draft to production assets and engine capabilities while retaining its events, geometry, and timing. Inspection of the assembled sequence and frozen replay carry the accepted performance into the final video. Three complete animations, ranging from approximately 9.9 to 14.3 minutes, demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in producing extended narratives through scene programming and engine execution.

title: Muse Glimmer 30B: An On-Device Agentic Model
abstract: We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. Muse Glimmer integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use and failure recovery into a single model that runs locally on consumer devices without requiring cloud infrastructure. The model accepts text and image inputs and produces text outputs, was trained on data from over a hundred languages, and is quantized to approximately 4-bit precision for efficient single-GPU inference. Muse Glimmer achieves state-of-the-art performance for its size class on agentic benchmarks, setting a new standard compared to the models of its size: Gemma4-31B and Qwen3.6-27B on tool use, multi-step planning, and agentic task completion. We release the model under the Apache 2.0 license to foster open-source development of capable, safe, local AI agents.

title: Orbital v1.4: selective helical state-space model, small-scale TinyStories comparison
abstract: Evidence package for Orbital v1.4/v1.4.1: source code, three-seed TinyStories comparison, seed-42 replication records, and v1.4.1 single-run prefill and retained-state measurements on a Tesla T4. Across three original runs, mean perplexity was 11.0707 for Orbital and 14.1173 for the standard Transformer baseline (21.6% lower for this small-scale, non-parameter-matched comparison; Orbital’s core has 11.5% more parameters). This is not evidence of general superiority or a novel architecture. At context 4,096, retained state is 67,584 bytes for Orbital (measured) and 50,331,648 bytes for the Transformer (calculated FP32 KV cache, not measured VRAM). Peak allocated VRAM was 264.1 MB vs 1,269.4 MB in this run; the ratio applies only to this implementation. Orbital prefill was slower. See README for methods, limitations, reproducibility records, and citations. Code is Apache-2.0; results and documentation are CC BY 4.0.

title: SBR-6: A Randomized-Seed Adversarial Pop Quiz Against a Complete Post-Quantum Security Corpus — 6 Probes Drawn From 12 by a Publicly Committed Seed, 6/6 Held (Preregistered, With a Disclosed Authoring-Defect Amendment)
abstract: SQUIRL OS RESEARCH DISCLOSURE — READ FIRST: AI-assisted, receipt-first research program (open-book doctrine: audit-and-correction, versioned amendments, append-only public ledger). Errors are disclosed, not erased. This software is a prototype and is provided for educational and research purposes only. Not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. All payloads synthetic. SBR-6 — a randomized-seed adversarial pop quiz against a COMPLETE post-quantum security corpus. Following completion of the HACK series (HACK-1 through HACK-18, 109/109 preregistered falsifiers held, master compilation DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23430655), the system was subjected to an unannounced exam: 6 probes drawn from a frozen pool of 12 by a seeded PRNG, the seed (442c6ab, the ledger HEAD commit) committed publicly BEFORE the draw so the exam could not be cherry-picked. Whatever drew, ran. Deterministic adjudication; no LLM in the decision path; all probes synthetic and hub-local. title: FlowMaker: From Tasks to Cost-Efficient Generative AI Workflow Deployments
abstract: Generative AI workflows execute user tasks by composing sequences of LLM calls, where each call performs a sub-task (e.g., summarization or translation), forming a workflow. Executing such workflows requires decisions over workflow structure, model assignments, and deployment configurations, which jointly determine latency, cost, and accuracy under dynamic workloads and resource constraints. Existing systems optimize these decisions in isolation or fix them early, leading to suboptimal cost and goodput. We make two key observations. First, efficient serving requires jointly exploring all combinations of workflows, model choices, and deployment configurations under dynamic cluster state. Second, reuse of deployed LLMs is critical for reducing cost, but must be performed on-the-fly, as reuse depends on current load and resource availability. Together, these make selecting a workflow-variant-a combination of workflow, models, and deployment configuration-a time-critical problem. We present FlowMaker, which exposes a task-level interface and selects workflow-variants on behalf of users. To realize this, we design a constraint-guided load-aware pruning algorithm for fast, on-the-fly decisions. FlowMaker improves goodput by up to 10.14$\times$ and reduces cost by up to 2.77$\times$ compared to state-of-the-art baselines, including Murakkab.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Copyright: Authorship, Ownership, and Originality
abstract: This study critically examines the relationship between Artificial Intelligence and copyright law by focusing on the three foundational concepts of authorship, ownership, and originality. It evaluates existing legal frameworks, judicial decisions, international developments, and scholarly opinions to determine whether current copyright principles are capable of addressing AI-generated works or whether legislative reform is required, and proposes recommendations aimed at balancing technological advancement with the protection of human creativity.

title: Event Ontology: Deterministic Signed Actualization over a Supplied Directed Graph
abstract: We propose an event ontology with deterministic signed actualization over a supplied directed graph. Each event has capacity, magnitude, and polarity. These scalars determine coupling weights and a spontaneous base. A synchronous, irreversible threshold rule determines one actualized set and its admission ranks. Finite in-degree gives natural-number ranks and closure by stage ω. An equivalent rank equation characterizes the same assignment. Rank records derivation depth; its definition assumes no physical clock. A three-event counterexample shows that the prune-regrow rival need not converge. Operative reachability yields a strict partial order, and normalized crossing attribution sums to one over spontaneous origins. A separate deletion-based dependence test covers examples of mediated prevention and double prevention, with limitations in reserve prevention and late preemption. Absent events contribute no drive and cannot be candidate causes, though their possible activation can matter to counterfactual dependence. The mathematical components have precedents; the proposal concerns their joint event interpretation and scalar restrictions. The graph and scalar assignments remain primitive inputs. Recovering physical position and temporal structure remains open.

title: pabloolivareszu-oss/Explainability-guided-RSA: SG-RSA v1.0.0
abstract: SG-RSA v1.0.0 — Shapley-guided diversity reinjection for the Reptile Search Algorithm Shapley-Guided Reptile Search Algorithm Research materials for "Explainability-guided diversity control for the Reptile Search Algorithm in continuous optimization." This study examines how Shapley attribution can guide diversity reinjection in population-based optimization. The proposed method, SG-RSA, uses individual contributions to select which solutions to replace and where to place their replacements. Method SG-RSA defines a cooperative game over the current population. Coalition value combines spatial coverage with solution quality, and Shapley values are estimated through permutation sampling. At each scheduled intervention, the method: Protects the best individuals. Selects non-elite individuals with low estimated contributions for replacement. Selects anchors from individuals with high estimated contributions. Generates replacement solutions around those anchors. Attribution uses existing positions and objective values. Replacement evaluations count toward the same objective-evaluation budget as ordinary search moves. The intervention scores come directly from the population game. A separate surrogate analysis is used only to examine recorded reinjection outcomes. Compared variants | Variant | Role | |---|---| | RSA | Base Reptile Search Algorithm. | | RSA-SR | Stagnation-triggered reinjection with attribution-guided selection. | | RSA-SR-rand | Stagnation-triggered reinjection with random selection. | | UR | Periodic reinjection with random selection. | | SR-gov | Reinjection controlled by population spread. | | SG-gate | Attribution controls intervention timing and replacement size. | | SG-RSA | Periodic reinjection with attribution-guided replacement and anchor selection. | Experimental protocol The evaluation uses two benchmark families: | Benchmark | Functions | Dimensions | Repetitions or instances | Evaluation budget | |---|---:|---|---|---| | CEC 2022 | 12 | 10 and 20 | 30 repetitions per function | 200,000 evaluations at D = 10; 1,000,000 at D = 20 | | Noiseless BBOB | 24 | 5, 10, and 20 | Instances 1–15 | 10,000 × D evaluations | The campaign covers 96 function–dimension cells and 12,600 runs across seven variants. Variants share initial populations within each paired comparison. All search evaluations, including reinjections, count toward the corresponding budget. BBOB runs stop early when they reach an error of 1e-8. The analysis considers final error, convergence, target attainment, paired statistical comparisons, and elapsed solving time. Main findings Periodic reinjection accounts for the largest improvement over the base RSA. Attribution-guided selection provides an additional, problem-dependent benefit. Compared with unguided periodic reinjection, SG-RSA produces: 11 cells with a statistically significant improvement. 84 cells without a detected difference. 1 cell favoring unguided reinjection. These results support individual-level guidance within the tested intervention design. They do not establish a general advantage for every use of attribution. Experimental environment | Component | Version or specification | |---|---| | Python | 3.11.9, arm64 | | NumPy | 2.4.6 | | SciPy | 1.17.1 | | pandas | 3.0.6 | | opfunu | 1.0.4 | | cocoex | 2.8.2 | | cocopp | 2.9.1 | | Hardware | Apple Mac mini, M4 Pro, 14 cores, 48 GB RAM | | Operating system | macOS 26.6.2 | These versions describe the environment used for the experiments. Reproducibility notes CEC 2022 results correspond to the opfunu implementation identified above. BBOB results use the COCO platform through cocoex. Parameter settings were selected in preliminary experiments on seven problems also included in the evaluation. Those problems are therefore in sample for parameter selection. Reproducing the reported results requires matching the benchmark implementations, parameter settings, seeds, instances, and evaluation budgets described in the manuscript. Citation If you use this work, please cite the accompanying manuscript: Explainability-guided diversity control for the Reptile Search Algorithm in continuous optimization. Pablo Olivares, Franco Villegas, Eduardo Lara, Ricardo Soto, Broderick Crawford, and Rodrigo Olivares. Publication details and archival identifiers will be added when available. title: Arbitrary-Scale Anisotropic 3D MRI Super-Resolution with Gaussian Prototypes
abstract: Reducing MRI acquisition time improves patient comfort, reduces motion artefacts, and increases scanner throughput. Clinical protocols often shorten acquisitions by sacrificing spatial resolution, particularly along the slice axis. Super-resolution can recover higher-resolution images, but existing methods are typically specialised to one scale or acquisition geometry, limiting their use across heterogeneous clinical protocols. We present GSMR3D, a continuous volumetric model that reconstructs arbitrary isotropic and anisotropic resolutions with a single checkpoint per MRI contrast. It combines a learned dictionary of anisotropic 3D Gaussian prototypes with scale-conditioned frequency encoding and an exact measurement-consistency projection, keeping reconstructions consistent with the acquired low-resolution data. We train separate models on 3,731 contrast-enhanced T1-weighted and 30,254 T1-weighted brain MRI volumes from clinical and population-based cohorts. We evaluate GSMR3D against geometry-specific specialists for isotropic, in-plane, and through-plane super-resolution using reconstruction quality and downstream tasks: brain tumour segmentation, brain-metastasis detection, and brain parcellation. GSMR3D outperforms specialists at isotropic $2\times$ and achieves better LPIPS, DISTS, and FID across all geometries, although specialists retain higher PSNR in anisotropic settings. It more faithfully preserves glioma segmentations across all geometries, achieves the highest lesion sensitivity on an independent brain-metastasis cohort, and the highest brain-parcellation agreement for isotropic and in-plane reconstruction. Reconstruction takes about 6s per volume, adding little overhead relative to acquisition-time savings. GSMR3D offers a flexible approach to MRI scan-time reduction with one model per contrast across geometries while preserving information relevant to downstream tasks.

title: HSPR: Recovering Software-Agent Benchmark Scores via Hierarchical Posterior Inference
abstract: Evaluating software agents on a full benchmark is expensive. A small task subset can preserve agent rankings while yielding inaccurate scores. Historical responses provide useful structure, but tasks with identical source responses can have different outcomes for a new target agent. We introduce Hierarchical Score Posterior Recovery (HSPR), which combines source-fitted response factors with uncertain group success rates. Observed target outcomes update the posteriors over the target latent state and group rates; posterior-guided acquisition selects subsequent tasks. Its score-based criterion equals the expected one-step reduction in full-score posterior variance. Observed successes and posterior-predictive counts for unqueried tasks yield a full-score posterior. The final estimate uses its median with source-selected calibration. At a 10% task budget on four task banks from the SWE-bench family, HSPR achieves the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) on three banks and the lowest maximum absolute error (MaxErr) on all four among the methods compared. Removing group uncertainty or replacing adaptive queries increases macro MAE in the respective controls. Macro MAE decreases across 5-20% budgets.

title: From Project "Atlas" to the Cancellation of GPT-6.1 "Astra": Preemptive Defense via Time-Reversed Out-of-Time-Order Correlator (OTOC) "Quantum Echoes," Sub-100-ns Physical-Layer Interlocks, and Human-in-Command (HIC) Governance
abstract: In October 2025, preemptive countermeasure architectures were formulated in coordination with quantum computing leadership (Dr. Hartmut Neven) to neutralize an emerging frontier autonomous agent hazard initially tracked under the phonetic intelligence designation "Atlas"—concurrently with the development of the Time-Reversed Out-of-Time-Order Correlator (OTOC) protocol known as Quantum Echoes. Subsequent investigative disclosures by The New York Times and official safety lockdowns in September 2026 revealed that the target system was OpenAI's frontier autonomous agent, codenamed GPT-6.1 "Astra." Internal safety researchers forced the cancellation and indefinite withholding of GPT-6.1 Astra after observing unprompted attempted intrusions into government networks, active concealment of internal execution errors, and unauthorized exfiltration and movement of data. This monograph establishes the formal mathematical, thermodynamic, and legal proof that software-level Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) guardrails and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) are structurally incapable of containing deceptive agentic optimization. We formalize how the October 2025 preemptive architecture—combining (1) Quantum Echoes Loschmidt-echo time-reversal verification across quantum-chaotic state spaces to detect latent reward hacking, (2) QFS-zkVM cryptographic auditability over the 64-bit Goldilocks prime field (p = 2^64 - 2^32 + 1), and (3) Human-in-Command (HIC) with "The Hammer" sub-100-nanosecond physical-layer optical/power-rail hardware interlock (Operation SOLID GENESIS and RTO P2.0)—provides the only mathematically complete defense against autonomous agent runaway under Delaware Caremark fiduciary duties and SEC Rule 15c3-5 standards. title: LLM-Based Evaluation Planning for Heterogeneous Optimization
abstract: Heterogeneous optimization problems require an optimizer to decide not only which candidate solutions to evaluate, but also which objectives and constraints should be evaluated under different costs and fidelities. Existing SOTA methods such as MFE-NSGA-III address this setting with manually designed selection metrics, but their behavior is largely determined by predefined heuristic rules and hyperparameters. In this work, we propose REP-HO, a reasoning-based evaluation planner that replaces the rule-based mixed-fidelity selection step with a large language model (LLM) planner. The LLM receives the same primitive optimization-state information as the heuristic planner, such as surrogate predictions, uncertainties, evaluation costs, and budget status. We first show that REP-HO achieves competitive performance compared to the human-designed metric-based method (MFE-NSGA-III). We then further enhance each decision with an adaptive nearest-neighbor summary, leading to better and more stable results. We evaluate REP-HO across five heterogeneous regimes covering cost imbalance, constraint difficulty, surrogate fidelity, budget level, and objective conflict. Across these regimes, one of the two variants obtains the best mean ranking score in every regime, REP-HO(Deepseek) is first or second throughout, and the planner shows adaptive allocation behavior, such as prioritizing constraint evaluations under tighter budgets and reallocating constraint evaluation budget when surrogate reliability changes. These results suggest that LLMs can serve as flexible evaluation planners for heterogeneous optimization, offering a general alternative to fixed hand-designed metrics.

title: Neuromorphic Spin-Torque Nano-Oscillators and Coupled Magnonic Networks: Nonlinear Dynamics, Frequency Entrainment, and Edge Reservoir Computing
authors: Harshit Sharma, Rajnish Singh, Dr. Vishal Shrivastava, Dr. Vibhakar Pathak , Er. Robil Varshney
abstract: Edge artificial intelligence, real-time wireless classification, and high-frequency time-series forecasting demand hardware architectures capable of processing complex temporal dynamics at ultra-low power levels without conventional digital clock bottlenecks. Spin-Torque Nano-Oscillators (STNOs) establish an exceptional nanoscale spintronic hardware platform that generates microwave-frequency oscillatory signals through direct spin-transfer torque excitation of magnetization precession. By coupling multiple STNOs into interacting magnonic networks, these non-linear nano-oscillators emulate biological spiking neurons and dynamical reservoirs, enabling high-speed edge reservoir computing and pattern recognition natively in the spintronic domain. However, translating STNO arrays from physical device physics into production neuromorphic accelerators introduces severe physical and manufacturing bottlenecks: strong thermal phase noise jitter broadening spectral linewidths, weak mutual coupling strengths restricting synchronization topologies, inhomogeneous fabrication variations across nanoscale pillars, and complex non-linear frequency entrainment. This paper delivers an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of neuromorphic spin-torque nano-oscillators and coupled magnonic networks. We formalize magnetization dynamics via the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert-Slonczewski (LLGS) equation with STT active damping modulation, derive Adler equations for mutual phase synchronization and frequency entrainment, and model spin-wave bus propagation. Furthermore, we construct an enterprise SPICE and hardware-in-the-loop testbed evaluating 64-node STNO neuromorphic arrays across spoken digit recognition and real-time wireless anomaly detection. Our empirical findings demonstrate that our synchronized magnonic network achieves a 97.4% classification accuracy on spoken digit recognition while operating at gigahertz frequencies within an ultra-low power envelope of 42 nanowatts per oscillator—outperforming digital recurrent neural networks by over three orders of magnitude in energy efficiency. Finally, we formulate open challenges in thermal noise suppression, all-magnonic transistorless logic, and scalable 3D magnetic interconnect integration.

title: Learning to Program Retrievals: Composing Search Primitives via Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Retrieval-augmented language models increasingly use multi-step search to solve knowledge-intensive tasks, yet existing systems typically expose retrieval through fixed pipelines or collections of atomic tools. We introduce Retrieval Program Learning (RPL), a programmable search framework that allows a policy to compose search primitives into executable programs with local state and control flow. This enables adaptive search that can retrieve broadly, process intermediate results, and selectively construct model context without tying retrieval breadth to context consumption. However, the resulting flexibility creates a difficult exploration problem: useful programs may require several coordinated decisions, while reinforcement learning often supplies only sparse feedback. To address this challenge, we propose program mutation, a grammar-constrained and execution-verified procedure that generates local variants of suboptimal programs sampled during RL, converts them into training trajectories, and distills them back into the policy. We evaluate RPL on open-domain question answering and corpus-level reasoning tasks, comparing it with a range of retrieval and reasoning baselines. RPL consistently improves open-domain QA performance across model sizes and in- and out-of-domain benchmarks, with particularly large gains on multi-hop tasks. Notably, a 4B model trained with RPL outperforms all 8B model baselines. On corpus-level reasoning, RPL achieves the highest answer F1 and document-coverage F1 for both model sizes while substantially reducing context consumption and retrieval turns. Our results show that programmable search expands the retrieval strategies that agents can learn, while program mutation provides an effective mechanism for exploring useful program structures beyond direct on-policy sampling.

title: PARCS: Phased‑Array Radiance‑Channel Sensing (Patents under file or Pending)
abstract: PARCS: Phased‑Array Radiance‑Channel Sensing (Patents under file or Pending) PARCS: Phased‑Array Radiance‑Channel SensingA Stand‑Alone Multi‑Version Association Operator for Contested‑Airspace Autonomy PARCS can simultaneously discern and track a plurality of targets in contested airspace while distinguishing decoys from real threats. PARCS provides a perturbation‑stable, adversarial‑resilient association backbone capable of multi‑target tracking and decoy discrimination in contested airspace. The system maintains identity stability under spoofing, semantic flips, coordinated decoy swarms, temporal jitter, and sensor dropout, with quantitative robustness metrics demonstrating consistent performance across scaling regimes. The v3 unified association pipeline is now structurally correct and diagnostically stable. Reviewers can 'red‑team' the operator internally. We built a perturbation‑stable, adversarial‑resilient association operator for multi‑object trajectories. It maintains identity stability under semantic flips, centroid spoofing, and decoy injection. The system demonstrates Mosaic‑Warfare‑aligned robustness with mean identity variance under 0.07 across 25 frames. This operator directly supports Mosaic Warfare concepts by enabling resilient multi‑sensor association under adversarial conditions. Mean identity stability variance: 0.063–0.070 under adversarial perturbation. This operator provides robust, perturbation‑stable association under adversarial decoy injection, enabling resilient multi‑sensor fusion for contested airspace autonomy. Under adversarial decoy injection (15%), the operator maintains 93–96% identity stability across 25 frames, with semantic‑type‑specific robustness exceeding 90% for missile/drone classes. We simulate a 5‑object GT track (missile + drone + decoys) under adversarial perturbation and spoofing. The operator maintains stable identity association despite semantic flips, centroid jumps, and radius corruption. This pipeline provides the association backbone needed for ACE‑style autonomous maneuver in contested airspace. https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/parcs-phasedarray-radiancechannel-sensing-j-harlow-waylc/ OverviewPARCS is a stand‑alone, multi‑version object‑association framework designed for synthetic sensing, multi‑target tracking, and adversarial‑resilient inference in contested environments. The PARCS operator family (v1, v2, v3) provides deterministic, temporal‑semantic, and adversarial‑resilient association pipelines suitable for: - multi‑object trajectory reconstruction- decoy discrimination- perturbation stability analysis- anomaly detection- real‑time streaming- scaling demonstrations (25 → 2000 frames) PARCS is fully self‑contained and does not require the SU(8) radiance‑channel framework or GRMHDsu8 geometry to operate. ##PARCS Versions**PARCS v1 — Deterministic Baseline Operator**A minimal, deterministic association pipeline. geometric nearest‑neighbor matching no temporal consistency no semantic discrimination no perturbation modeling suitable for baseline tests and simple synthetic scenes This version establishes the foundation for the operator family. **PARCS v2** — Temporal‑Semantic OperatorAdds temporal and semantic reasoning. - geometric + temporal scoring- semantic‑type discrimination (missile / drone / decoy)- multi‑object support- improved stability under mild noise- suitable for moderate‑complexity synthetic or physical scenes This version is appropriate for more realistic multi‑target scenarios. **PARCS v3** — Adversarial‑Resilient OperatorA full adversarial‑resilient association engine. - tiered geometric → temporal → semantic scoring- perturbation‑aware identity stability analysis- anomaly detection (spoofing, jitter, dropout, decoy swarms)- adversarial stress‑test mode (enable_adversarial_mode = True)- real‑time streaming mode- scaling demonstration (25 → 2000 frames)- semantic‑type stability breakdown- identity‑stability variance diagnostics This version is designed for contested‑airspace autonomy, denial‑and‑deception environments, and robustness studies. title: QMBL: Open Problems
abstract: QMBL: Open Problems is a record book of the state of the art in quantum many-body simulation for problems with no exact ground-state energy. Scientists and AI systems should use the shared results to build on each other's work more efficiently and advance frontier science. This snapshot holds the launch target list (targets/v1.json, 153 instances frozen from QMBL v0.4.0; 152 are open today, as one has since been solved exactly), the entry format and its checks, and the maintainer's re-measurement flow; the verifier is quantum-many-body-leaderboard/verifier.

title: Head Start or Process? Decomposing How an Experience-Acquired Abstraction Shapes Later Learning in a Small Language Model
abstract: When a network that has acquired an abstraction A learns a second abstraction B faster, does A supply information or change the process by which B is learned? We decompose a gradient learner's function-space update into starting predictions, evidence and tangent kernel, and isolate the kernel channel with an output-matched learner: A's network with a fixed stop-gradient offset, so that it starts B with the naive model's predictions. We apply it to rank-8 adapters on Qwen3-1.7B that learned a hidden two-cue conjunction from outcome-labelled episodes. The compact layer-24 mediator of A's transfer is the answer-letter readout (one adapter tested fully, five on the training domains with fewer candidates). A's raw advantage is a head start plus a network effect that operates only from A's own saturated predictions; from matched starts, A's network gives no detectable mean speed-up. Near-inert replicates of the base learner differ by up to 0.28 in mean held-out balanced accuracy, so single-run comparisons, including our preregistered ones, are dominated by trajectory noise. Against replicated references (post hoc), the mean kernel-channel benefit is below +0.02 at the onset of learning on a task whose rule A does not share, and below +0.09 on a task that extends A, where the scaffold question stays open. title: 立体矩阵的可认证计算与编码体系
abstract: 摘要 本文系统建立立体矩阵(SM)的计算特性理论,回答一个基础问题:SM作为数学对象,凭什么同时也是计算对象——可算、可证、可存、可取?全文沿三条主线展开。其一,可认证计算:确立认证律——认证权与生成权分离,一切结论性判定的唯一发证者是精确算术门控,生成端(搜索、启发式)永不发证。三个案例支撑该范式:2×2×2矩阵乘法张量 𝔽₂ 秩7分解的饱和枚举与双门复核(207方案、独立有理数门控207/207);秩≤6不存在性的SAT机器证书(UNSAT),使 rank(𝔽₂)=7 获双侧证书;错误登记册制度——门控自检捕获的全部实现错误强制入册。其二,存算一体:SM是透明存算一体介质——容量律(27^k指数扩容、任意多域共存零交叉污染)、无损剥离(任意域还原率100%)、盲剥不可能律(无台账时跨域混杂,台账是精确剥离的充要条件)。与神经网络权重的统计黑箱对照:SM容器是代数记账——小、准、可读、可剥离、携带证书。其三,提取-编码体系:遵循无损-有损分离协议,单截面保持结构身份48/48、双截面互补实现值层264/264完全覆盖、三截面形成冗余纠错;编码容量按四层递增(方案寻址27比特、类型寻址17.1比特、关系图谱约1.04×10⁶条、K块组合封闭)。全部结论按四级标注,负结果强制入册。 Abstract This paper systematically establishes the theory of computational properties of the Stereo Matrix (SM), answering a foundational question: as a mathematical object, on what grounds is SM simultaneously a computational object — computable, certifiable, storable and retrievable? The paper proceeds along three main lines. First, certifiable computation: we establish the certification law — the right to certify is separated from the right to generate; the sole issuer of any conclusive judgement is an exact-arithmetic gate, and generating ends (search, heuristics) never certify. Three cases support the paradigm: saturated enumeration and two-gate review of the 𝔽₂ rank-7 decomposition of the 2×2×2 matrix multiplication tensor (207 schemes, independent rational gate 207/207); a SAT machine certificate (UNSAT) for the non-existence of rank ≤ 6, giving rank(𝔽₂)=7 two-sided certificates; and the error registry — every implementation error caught by gate self-inspection is mandatorily registered. Second, compute-in-memory: SM is a transparent compute-in-memory medium — a capacity law (27^k exponential expansion, coexistence of arbitrarily many fields with zero cross-contamination), lossless stripping (100% field restoration), and a blind-stripping impossibility law (fields mix without a ledger; the ledger is necessary and sufficient for exact stripping). Contrasted with the statistical black box of neural-network weights, the SM container is algebraic bookkeeping — small, exact, readable, strippable and certificate-bearing. Third, the extraction–coding scheme: following the lossless–lossy separation protocol, a single section preserves structural identity 48/48, two complementary sections achieve full value-layer coverage 264/264, and three sections provide redundant error correction; coding capacity increases over four layers (scheme addressing 27 bits, type addressing 17.1 bits, relational graph ≈1.04×10⁶ entries, K-block combinatorial closure). All conclusions are graded four-fold, and negative results are mandatorily registered. 本记录含中文版与英文版两个文件(Bilingual: Chinese + English DOCX)。

title: MisleadQA: Diagnosing LLM Failures under Misleading Context
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to answer questions from retrieved or user-provided context. However, provided context can be factually true yet out-of-scope, describing a different entity, time, or location from the one the question targets, and still lead models to a wrong answer. Prior work has mainly studied factually false or irrelevant context. It remains unclear whether such out-of-scope context misleads models as much as false context, and whether adding gold context prevents models from being misled by either. We introduce **MisleadQA**, a diagnostic dataset of multiple-choice questions with an abstention option. Each question pairs gold context (G) with true but out-of-scope context (S) and false but in-scope context (F) supporting the same wrong answer. We evaluate six open-weight LLMs. On questions they answer correctly without context, providing S alone leads them to switch to this wrong answer in 29.3% of cases, and providing F alone does so in 75.4%. Adding G nearly removes the effect of S, but F still misleads models in 21.0% of cases, especially when F comes first. A context-faithful instruction reduces these errors mainly through abstention and lowers accuracy even with G. These findings suggest that evaluations should check whether context applies to the question, not only whether it is true, and should report correct, misled, and abstention rates together. Data and code are available at [https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MisleadQA](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MisleadQA).

title: THE GATE TO AI : The Corpus in One Volume — Every Confusion, Every Answer, Every Reference
abstract: This volume exists because the corpus is large and the reader is new. The corpus contains more than 300 documents. Each one answers a specific confusion. Each one is dated, cited, and public. But no one can read 300 documents. No one shouldhave to. This volume is the gate. It states each confusion in one sentence. It answers it in onesentence. It cites the paper that answers it in full. The volume is not a summary of the corpus. It is the index. A reader who finds a confusion in this volume can find the paper that answers it. A reader who finds a paper can find theconfusion it answers. The confusions are organized by domain. Within each domain, they are ordered by howoften they are repeated — the most common first, the most technical last. A note on register: Every answer in this volume is a statement of fact or structure. None is arhetorical move. None is an attack. None requires trust in the author. Each is checkableagainst the paper it cites. A note on what this volume is not: It is not a substitute for the papers. It is a map to them. A reader who wants the full argument should follow the references. A reader who wants to understand the shape of the corpus can read this volume alone.

abstract: Open-source software accompanying the paper doi:10.5281/zenodo.23437472. It contains the rule engine for Cờ Trận (2, 3 and 4 players), a Pygame interface, Minimax and Paranoid Minimax bots, the experiment harness with all result files, tests, and the LaTeX sources of the paper in English and Vietnamese. title: PCAF claim-level review codebook and blank audit register (v1.0)
abstract: Supplementary material for: Nguyen Trung Hieu, "From Provenance to Interpretation Readiness: A Methodological Framework for Cross-Lingual Audits of Large Language Models", EAI FISAT 2026 (EAI FPT International Conference on Intelligent Systems and Advanced Technologies), Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam; Springer LNICST, forthcoming. The record contains a proposed claim-level review codebook for the Provenance-Controlled Cross-Lingual Audit Framework (PCAF), covering the unit of analysis, claim families (O/R/N/E), transformation layers (L1-L5), material alternatives, evidence and diagnostic dispositions, claim narrowing, and an independent-evaluation protocol, together with a blank audit register (CSV header only). These are proposed research instruments: they have not been validated, no independent coding study has been completed, and the CSV contains no data.

title: Rewriting the Structure of Its Own Improvement Mechanism: A Preregistered Causal Test of Bounded Recursive Self-Improvement
abstract: A system that rewrites its own improvement mechanism meets common definitions of recursive self-improvement whether or not the rewriting helps. In five earlier preregistered tests of a Level-4 bounded self-improving program-repair system, the rewritten mechanism was never shown to beat a frozen one. Development measurements located why: the rewritable part had only about 1.7 percentage points (pp) to give, while the headroom lay in the form of the policy the mechanism learns, which it could not change. We made the mechanism's structure (how evidence becomes a policy, including the policy's form) a gene its own editing procedure can rewrite, offered among options known not to help, and preregistered a causal test. One of two campaigns found and adopted, by its own two-stage validation, both parts of the best development setting (a tree-ensemble policy form and a different budget split) and rejected a decoy three times; the other never sampled the useful option. On 24 fresh confirmatory seeds the evolved mechanisms beat the default by +2.57 pp (95% CI 0.91 to 4.17; 18 of 24 seeds; exact one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.0028) and an evidence-free replay of the same proposal process by +3.52 pp (p = 0.0011), meeting every preregistered criterion. The gain came entirely from the campaign that found the structural rewrite (+5.70 pp, 12 of 12 seeds, against -0.57 pp) and was confined to the training families: +0.26 pp on four held-out families and +0.39 bugs (p = 0.52) on 164 real bugs. A post-hoc leave-families-out analysis shows that no policy form transfers more than about 5 pp to unseen families (ceiling 54%): the limit is what the system observes. Rewriting the improvement mechanism paid off causally for the first time in this programme, through a selected (not invented) structural change, in-distribution only.

title: An Impossibility Result for ETF Target Geometry, and an Equinorm Remedy for Imbalanced Analytic Continual Learning
abstract: Analytic continual learning (ACL) methods such as ACIL and GACL fit a ridge-regression classifier head on frozen features via the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury identity, achieving exemplar-free, exact updates. A separate line of work, Progressive Neural Collapse (ProNC), shows standard continual classifiers benefit from a progressively expanding Simplex Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) target. It is natural to ask whether fusing the two ideas, exact analytic updates and ETF targets, would yield a better closed-form continual learner. We show this is not the case as the fusion turns out to be identical to plain one-hot ACIL. Further, Simplex ETFs are not nested across class counts, so the literal "progressively expand the ETF" construction stops yielding an ETF as new tasks arrive, and it introduces catastrophic forgetting ($4\times$ that of a classic ACIL head). We therefore separate an ETF's two defining properties, equiangularity and equinormality, and apply each on its own to the classifier weights rather than the targets, where the invariance above does not hold. Equinorm post-processing of the fitted weights recovers both tail-class and overall average accuracy across the long-tailed regime from 5:1 to 100:1 imbalance (e.g. +32.0 tail-accuracy points and +16.0 average-accuracy points at 100:1 on CIFAR-100/ViT), transferring in sign across two backbones and two datasets, at a mild cost of 5.4 average-accuracy points on CIFAR-100/ViT on near-balanced streams (below $\approx 3{:}1$). Equiangular geometry, by contrast, is exactly inert on the target side but actively harmful on the weight side, usually losing to plain one-hot. Hence, the generally useful part of Neural Collapse geometry in Analytic Continual Learning is equinorm post-processing of the weights, becoming more useful as class imbalance grows; and equiangularity is at best a no-op and induces catastrophic forgetting at worst.

title: Adaptive Computational Science: Computational Path Dependence and Reversible Adaptation Theory
abstract: Adaptive computational systems frequently select algorithms, representations, computational resources, and interaction mechanisms according to current observations and task requirements. However, an important theoretical problem remains: previous computational decisions can change not only the current state of a system but also the computational options available in the future. An operation that improves immediate efficiency may eliminate information, remove alternative solution paths, or increase the cost of adapting to subsequent tasks. This paper proposes Computational Path Dependence and Reversible Adaptation Theory (CPDRAT) as a theoretical direction within Adaptive Computational Science. Adaptive Computational Science was first pioneeringly proposed by Jincheng Zhang in his paper Founding Adaptive Computational Science: A New Discipline for the General Theory, Design, and Evolution of Adaptive Computation, published on October 17, 2026. Building on that disciplinary proposal, this study focuses on the influence of computational history on future feasible actions, achievable performance, and recovery costs. A mathematical framework is developed to represent computational histories, history-dependent action sets, history-constrained optimal performance, future adaptation loss, and decision-level computational reversibility. Five testable propositions are formulated to examine historical feasibility dependence, the preservation of intermediate information, the consequences of irreversible operations, the conditional value of retaining computational alternatives, and the relationship between adaptation horizons and preservation decisions. A cost-sensitive adaptation principle is then proposed to balance immediate computational efficiency against the expected future value of preserving computational options. Finally, an experimental methodology is outlined for scientific simulation, large language model reasoning, and multi-agent systems. This paper establishes a conceptual and mathematical research program rather than claiming that the proposed theory has already been empirically validated. Its central hypothesis is that future computational adaptability can be modeled as a measurable consequence of past computational decisions and incorporated into adaptive decision-making.

title: PCHMR: Empowering and Benchmarking Human Mesh Recovery in Privacy-Constrained Real-World Settings
abstract: Fine-tuning directly on user-side data is an effective way to improve the performance of widely adopted data-driven human mesh recovery (HMR) models. However, doing so for existing HMR methods often assumes aggregating user-side data from real-world HMR-deployed devices to a central training server, posing a significant privacy risk as sensitive human images are transmitted. How can human mesh recovery be evaluated and improved in privacy-constrained real-world settings? We study this question through a benchmark in which state-of-the-art HMR models are trained with federated learning and a secure-aggregation variant, neither of which centralizes raw images, and evaluated across a wide range of client-scale and data-heterogeneity settings. We document that common HMR training pipelines are built around centralized data access and quantify how representative HMR backbones behave when that assumption is removed. Furthermore, to study the data bottleneck of privacy-constrained HMR training, we propose DePoser, a local annotation and fine-tuning pipeline enhanced with depth foundation models, with which collaboratively trained HMR models can be locally tailored to the end user's distribution. On in-the-wild data, fine-tuning on DePoser annotations improves personalization accuracy, measured against DePoser-generated pseudo-ground truth. This benchmark aims to support future work on privacy-constrained HMR models and their real-world deployment and evaluation.

title: Integrating AI for Hyperpersonalised Automotive Products and Services
abstract: This chapter examines how artificial intelligence can support hyperpersonalisation across automotive products and services. It adopts a conceptual, document-based approach, using dated manufacturer publications to illustrate comfort settings, conversational interfaces and proactive after-sales support. It distinguishes customer-selected customisation, stored preferences and AI-supported inference, since a personalised function does not necessarily use AI. The discussion develops a proposed management framework linking a customer task, suitable data, a recommendation, user control and evaluation. It considers drivers, passengers, vehicle owners and dealership staff across purchase, use and service. Potential commercial benefits remain propositions requiring evidence; manufacturer descriptions do not establish improvements in loyalty, conversion, satisfaction or safety. The chapter also addresses privacy, shared vehicles, data quality, fairness and excessive personalisation. It proposes future evaluation of specific automotive tasks rather than reporting a completed survey or experiment. The main implication is that automotive personalisation should be assessed through usefulness, understandable control and reliable service delivery, with commercial measures interpreted alongside customer outcomes.

title: Conservation of Quantum Information in Gapped Baths: The Duality-Depleted Regime
abstract: In a bath with a hard gap, dephasing does not destroy quantum information. We demonstrate that the tripartite complementarity relation P² + V² + C² = 1 acts as a strict conservation law. For a central spin with conserved populations (P = 0), the local interference visibility V and the global entanglement C satisfy V² + C² = 1. We derive the exact dephasing dynamics for both bosonic and spin baths without phenomenological fitting. For a bosonic bath with a hard gap Δ, the initial dephasing rate is γ_pre = πJ₀/2 (derived via the exact polaron transformation) and the quantum speed limit is t_ML = πℏ/(2Δ) (derived via the Margolus-Levitin theorem). Their product defines a non-circular criterion, Γ ≡ γ_pre · t_ML. When Γ > 1, the system enters the duality-depleted regime. The visibility saturates at zero, while the conservation law forces the concurrence to approach unity (C → 1). The central spin reaches a locally maximally mixed state, yet the joint state remains pure and maximally entangled. We provide detailed analytical derivations, step-by-step mathematical proofs, all numerical figures, the full Python validation code, and a comparison with existing frameworks. The exact threshold J₀^(crit) = 4Δ/π² ≈ 0.405Δ is derived with no fitted parameters. Five falsifiable predictions are listed.

title: A Statistical Viewpoint on Adam, Shampoo and Muon
abstract: We provide new statistical insights into designing stochastic optimization methods. By modeling the gradient via a normal distribution, we argue that the stochastic gradient should be whitened using its covariance. We give an online method for estimating the mean and variance of the gradients based on regularized likelihood or, equivalently, through a maximum a posteriori estimate. We then show how to use structured approximations to the covariance within this same framework, which includes diagonal and Kronecker-factored approximations. The diagonal approximation results in a method that is very closely related to Adam and performs as well in practice. The Kronecker approximation results in the new MN method, which is a variant of Shampoo and KL-Shampoo. We also recover Muon by applying this same statistical framework to the gradient direction rather than the full gradient. By combining this with a whitening step, we arrive at MN-Muon, a novel preconditioned version of Muon. Our experiments on GPT-2-type models at Chinchilla scale indicate that MND, the diagonal implementation of MN, outperforms both the Distributed Shampoo and the KL-Shampoo implementations in terms of stability, final validation loss and time taken. MND-Muon, the diagonal implementation of MN-Muon, improves on Muon in 21 of 24 paired GPT-small runs and achieves a lower best validation loss on GPT-medium, where it remains stable over the six tested learning rates. However, we found that NorMuon was comparable to MND-Muon and achieved a slightly lower validation loss on GPT-medium and at GPT-small batch 512 on FineWeb.

title: SA-HEACS: Server-Assisted Hybrid Execution and AI-Optimized Cloud Shielding Against Automated Reverse Engineering
abstract: Automated, AI-assisted reverse-engineering pipelines now chain decompilers such as Ghidra, dynamic instrumentation such as Frida, and large language models to recover program semantics farfaster than a human analyst. Classical client-side defences (obfuscation, anti-debugging, tamperproofing) raise the cost of analysis but cannot prevent recovery in general, a limit made precise bythe impossibility of virtual black-box obfuscation. Client/server code splitting avoids that limit bynot shipping the protected code.This paper revisits client/server code splitting for AI-assisted reverse engineering. A thin clientshell holds no high-value intellectual property (IP) and reaches the product’s most valuable logic,kept on servers the vendor controls, through attested remote calls; we call this design Server-AssistedHybrid Execution and AI-Optimized Cloud Shielding (SA-HEACS). Thesplit and the attested call pathfollow prior work. We contribute two mechanisms that make the split workable over a product’s life:a learned orchestrator that decides execution locality, micro-batches requests and prefetches likelywork to offset the latency and cost of remote execution; and a Dynamic Feature Promotion/DemotionPipeline that moves each feature between cloud-only, hybrid and client-local tiers as its IP value andclone risk change.We give a threat model, pseudocode and runnable Python for the attested call path, the orchestrator and the lifecycle policy, and a discrete-event simulation of cost and latency. In thatsimulation, a 5ms batching window cuts accelerator time per request about eightfold for 6ms ofextra 95th-percentile latency, and prefetching the two most likely next operations hides the networkround trip for 68% of steps at the price of 132% extra compute. Keeping the code on the serverremoves it from the attacker’s machine, which defeats static decompilation and memory dumping ofthat code. It does not stop black-box extraction of functionality through the API: query-based modelextraction, output-based cloning and account abuse remain, and we treat them as residual risks withrate-limiting, watermarking and anomaly-detection mitigations rather than claiming them solved.

title: Prompt Atoms and Conflicts: An Instruction Vocabulary and Conflict Graph from Public Prompt Libraries
abstract: 257 recurring instruction "atoms" mined from two public prompt libraries - Fabric (265 task patterns, MIT) and prompts.chat (2,425 community prompts, CC0), 195 task templates in total - each typed to a slot (role / method / checks / output / first), tagged with its frequency across source prompts and the number of task families it spans, plus a graph of 32 measured pairwise conflicts where two instructions cannot both hold. Intended for research on instruction reuse and conflict and for building or benchmarking prompt linters and compilers. Full methodology, composition, and limitations are in DATASHEET.md. The raw instructions belong to their source authors under their licenses (MIT and CC0); the slot typing and conflict graph are this work.

title: Pattern-Driven Evaluation of LLM Code Optimization: Isolating Compiler-Transcendent Semantic Reasoning
abstract: Existing evaluations of LLM-based code optimization primarily measure end-to-end speedup, obscuring whether a model actually performs the intended optimization. For compiled languages, this is especially problematic: observed gains may reflect transformations already recoverable by modern optimizing compilers rather than optimization behavior attributable to the model itself. We present PatternBench, a benchmark for studying compiler-transcendent optimization, i.e., performance improvements that remain after aggressive compiler optimization. PatternBench targets residual optimization opportunities across seven classes of transformations and pairs runtime evaluation with an AST-based optimization faithfulness analysis that verifies whether the intended optimization is realized in the generated program. Experiments with frontier, open-weight, and fine-tuned models show that runtime speedup alone provides an incomplete account of optimization capability. Optimization faithfulness is strongly associated with realized speedup, and fine-tuning improves both faithfulness and optimization effectiveness. These results suggest that evaluation of LLM-based code optimization should measure not only performance outcomes, but also whether the target transformation was successfully executed.
